.AUTHORIZATION OF APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY MINISTERS FOR TAXATION AND CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
Hon, C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 108, to amend the Department -of National Revenue Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, owing to the appointment of Mr. Hugh D. Scully as consul general in New York there is a vacancy in the office of commissioner of customs. This bill provides for the combining of the office of [DOT]commissioner of customs with that of commissioner of excise and raising the status of the commissioner to that of a deputy minister. It also provides for raising the status of the [DOT]commissioner of income tax and succession [DOT]duties to that of a deputy minister.
Section 2 of the bill is to authorize the Minister of National Revenue to administer certain sections of the Special War Revenue Act. Under the Department of National Revenue Act the . minister is responsible for administering sections 4 to 14 of the Special War Revenue Act. This bill places section 2 and sections 15, 16 and 17 of the Special War Revenue Act under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Revenue.

Certainly not.

speechtext:
Order. The question is one to which the hon. member cannot expect an answer to-day. I have already brought to the attention of the house, not only during last session but also in this session, the matter of questions on the orders of the day. It is quite evident that many of these questions which are being asked, even though they are drafted as notice of motion to the ministers concerned, are not in accordance with the rules of the house. Any question requiring the deliberation of a minister or his department should be placed upon the order paper so that the minister and the department may have an opportunity to reply.
I may say at the same time that it is again becoming a general practice to refer to telegrams, reports in newspapers, and things of the kind which are reported in the daily press, and make them the subjects of questions on the floor of the house, although such questions cannot and should not be answered on the orders of the day. I would ask the house and I would ask hon. members who may be inclined to indulge in this practice to have some consideration not only for the Chair, who dislikes extremely to be always interrupting on these orders of the day, but to have regard for the rules of the house, with which all hon. members are conversant, and I think they ought to support the Chair in the attitude he is endeavouring to adopt.

I should like as the leader of the house to support what His Honour the Speaker has just said about the observance of rules and regulations, particularly as to the asking of questions on the orders of the day. I do that at this moment, because I know hon. members are hoping that we shall reach before long a stage when we will begin to wind up the business of this session. I think I may be able by conference with leaders of the different sides of the house to work toward that end without depriving any hon. members of full opportunities to discuss the questions which they wish to discuss. There are times and places to ask questions. Many of the questions which are being asked on the orders of'the day should either appear on the order paper or might be taken up when the affairs of the departments are under consideration.
The Speaker has referred to the practice of reading telegrams and extracts from newspapers and of basing questions thereon. Hon. members are aware that this is against the rules of the house. I believe that we shall all gain in the end if there is a close observance of the rules in that particular. Hon. members will be interested, I believe, in looking over Hansard, to see how much time has been taken up each week by questions that have been asked on the orders of the day, practically any of which, with one or two exceptions, might have been put upon the order paper and answered in the regular way. We are in this-position in the house at the present time, that the government faces really four oppositions, if not more, and when one opposition raises a question, if it happens to be the official opposition, very often members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party feel that they too must ask some question or other arising out of that one, and our friends of the Social Credit group have similar feelings and wish to ask questions-[DOT]

speechtext: Item 4.

I wanted to say a few words when the estimates of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services were under consideration before, but I was not able to do so; some of the long distance speakers got in before me. Yesterday the radio committee met while the house was in session and I hope that I am not out of order now in what I am going to say, because it would probably have come in better under one of the earlier items.
Some hon. members who have spoken on this question have come from the east coast and the west coast. May I point out that Alberta has done its part. In fact, all the western provinces have had their share in naval affairs, although we are far from either sea. In the prairie provinces we have 502 officers and 12,302 ratings, and the province of Alberta has led with 164 officers and 4,436 ratings, even though, as I say, we are a long distance from either ocean. Our men have taken part in the rigors of training, in the hardships of convoys, in the perils of combat. Our men have taken their share in the work and danger, in the deeds of gallantry and, at times, in the sacrifices that had to be made. We honour these men equally with the men of the air force and of the army, and I believe that those who have not yet had a chance to show what they can do will do so later and they will prove their worth.
I wanted to ask this question of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. Our men from. Alberta, particularly those in the navy, when on leave have to travel a long distance from either coast, and I wonder if the minister would consider the question of free transportation for sailors on leave. This question was brought up before when the estimates of the Minister of National Defence were under review. I suggested that if free transportation could not be given, at any rate a ceiling should be put on railway fares so that men from the central provinces would not have to spend a couple of months' pay when coming home on leave. I hope the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services will consider the question.

War Appropriations-Naval Services
May I speak again of the women in uniform. It is true that they are not in combat, not in actual physical danger, but if. they take the place of those who are fighting, then it seems to me that they should be given the recognition which that deserves. I wanted to bring these two matters to the attention of the minister.
I do not think that we need fear that, our men and women in uniform in any of the forces will let us down in the hour of combat, but we must see that they get the proper backing at home, not only from those who work in our shops or on our farms but from those who talk. It seems to me that in this connection we in this house have a definite duty to perform in the winning of the war. We should look at the matter in :a broad light and not with too much detail, and try to keep up the morale of our people at home and abroad. Surely Mr. Churchill's winged words have shown more than anything else how much the morale of a country can be increased by those who talk.

While the minister is pro-' tecting his navy and explaining the service they have been giving to this country, he has received splendid support from the government. I should like to announce something that appears in this morning's papers, that the corvette Port Arthur has sunk another submarine and has sent it to the same place it sent the last one. I want to congratulate the minister from Port Arthur.

I should like to ask the minister whether the purchase of property and the construction of buildings is entirely under his department or whether there is an association with the Department of Munitions and Supply or the Department of Public Works in that connection? Has the minister's department been offered the use of any large residences in the city of Winnipeg, for a small consideration, for the housing of Wrens, and is it the decided policy of the minister's department that in all such cases these houses must be either rented or purchased outright?
I had another question to ask yesterday but, like the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Casselman), I was attending a meeting of the committee on agriculture, which sat during the afternoon. Would the minister give the number of commissioned naval officers now stationed in Ottawa, or at headquarters?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall come to my hon. friend's questions in due course, but first I think I should answer those asked yesterday, in the order in which they were asked.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
First, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) raised the question of free transportation for men in the naval service. The same question was discussed this afternoon by the hon. member for Edmonton East. The giving of free transportation to sailors would have to go along with free transportation for the other services. I can assure my hon. friends that the matter has been discussed frequently by the three defence ministers, but up to the present time the provisions which have been made seem to be about as far as we can go. I shall be glad, however, to take the matter up again with my colleagues, to see whether anything further can be done.
Then the hon. member for Cape Breton South asked some questions about merchant shipping, and the records of men serving. Strictly speaking, that question should be answered by the Department of Transport. Mr. Arthur Randles, of that department, who is director of merchant seamen, can, I am sure, deal with it. There is a record of all merchant seamen who sign on through w'hat we call the manning pools, and the ships in which they serve are known. There is also a central index of seamen made in the Department of Transport by Mr. J. G. Macphail, director of marine sendees.
The hon. member wanted to know why some nurses were taken on and some rejected. The answer is that we have at least 2,500 applications from nurses in Canada who wish to join the naval nursing sendee, but up to date we have been able to take on only 132. It is obvious therefore that some must be disappointed. Other things being equal,
I would say first come first served would be the rule. But we have to remember that, some of those who apply have just graduated, while others have had four or five or sometimes ten years' experience. Naturally those with the longer experience would be favoured.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) raised some points of great interest-and raised them very fairly, as he always does. He wanted to know whether throughout the empire there was a uniform system of training, organization and the like.
I believe throughout all empire navies the model and the plan used in Great Britain would be followed pretty generally. We would use the admiralty textbooks to a very large extent, and from this country at any rate there is always some interchange of officers with the British navy. I would not say of course that we could not vary that procedure or that British practice if we 
desired to do so. But generally speaking I think it will be found that the training of all empire navies is very similar.
The hon. member wanted to know if there was a central board controlling empire navies. My answer is, no.
In respect of the other dominions-other than Canada-is there such a central authority?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not think so, although I have not looked into it. For instance I believe Australia, would run its own navy. However, if a section of the Canadian or the Australian navy went to serve with a part of the British navy, thereby becoming part of the British force, they would normally be under the command of the senior British officer.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) wanted to know something about the proportion of officers to men and pointed out what is quite true, namely, that some provinces have a very large proportion of officers to men as compared with other provinces. I think one of the explanations for that state of affairs would be that there are enlisted now in the Canadian Navy nearly one thousand officers of the merchant marine service. I should think the great majority of those officers would be from British Columbia, from the great lakes, Quebec and the maritime provinces. Most of the thousand men would come from those areas, thereby increasing the quota of officers from the provinces concerned. I would say to the hon. member how-ever that in the training under the new system everybody starts in at the lower deck and works up to his commission; and under it there would seem to be no reason why the best men should not rise to the top. I am sure that under this new system men from the western provinces will prove themselves worthy of commissions- to the same extent as men from the other provinces.
The hon. member for Bow River also raised a question as < to the differential in allowances as between certain men in the naval service, pointing out that some are getting $1.45 a day as living allowance while certain others get only $1.25. The hon. member is right in that; that is a true statement. But may I say that when we took up the question of pay in the navy and endeavoured in some way to make the rates of pay in the three armed services uniform we found that some of our men were getting more pay and some were getting less than their corresponding army or air force brothers. AVe found that while we were paying $1.45 a.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
day for subsistence to sailors the army was paying only a dollar-I believe it was a dollar. And so when we said that the pay of certain junior officers, which was very low in comiparison with other services, should be raised, we were confronted with the fact that these men, ordinary sailors in the navy, who were on subsistence were getting 45 cents a day more than army men on subsistence. What 'happened was that army men on subsistence were raised to $1.25 a day, and all men joining the navy after that date, June 1 of last year, were also given $1.25 a day. However we did not reduce the allowance of the men .who had already been in the navy, because we felt they had joined on the understanding that they were to be given $1.45 a day subsistence and that it would be unfair to rpduce them at some later time during their period of service.
The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) asked as to the training of merchant mariners, and a good many other questions as to sea cadets. As to merchant mariners, the naval service does give gunnery training to merchant seamen who are to form part of the gun crews of merchant ships. That training is given to Canadian merchant seamen and the merchant seamen of our allied countries who are in Canadian ports No other type of training is given by the navy to merchant seamen.
The hon. member also wanted to know how many civilians were active in organizing sea cadet corps throughout the country. There are two that are particularly active. I do not attempt to mention all those excellent men in different localities such as are to be found in my hon. friend's own city, Winnipeg, Toronto and other cities where there are sea cadet corps. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) mentioned that they had been interested in sea cadet work. I regret that I cannot give the names of all those who have taken a great interest in this work, but the two chief organizers who range over the country at large are Mr. R. C. Stevenson of Montreal, who is called coordinator of sea cadet activities-he gives his services free, receiving only travelling expenses-and Mr. J. R. K. Millen, who has particularly charge of the western sea cadet corps.
My hon. friend also wanted to know where the sea cadet camps would be. I have a list of the camps here, but it might be added to later. There are to be camps at Comox, British Columbia; Chestermere lake, near Calgary; lake Wabamun, near Edmonton; Shepley island, on the Saskatchewan river; Stevenson's Point, on lake Winnipeg; lake
Eva, 125 miles west of Port Arthur; Goderich, Ontario; Beausoleil island, in Georgian bay; Rotary island, near Gananoque; Minnicog island, in Georgian bay; Isle St. Quentin, near Three Rivers; Camp Buchan, in the Northumberland strait, thirty-one miles east of Charlottetown; Cole Harbour, twelve miles from Halifax. There is also to be a camp for the St. Lawrence cadet corps but I have not information as to just where it is to be.
The total number of cadets going to these camps, according to my figures, will be 2,275. That is the accommodation of these camps in their entirety. Some camps remain open longer than others. The usual camp period is two weeks. Some camps propose to give three two-week periods, while others propose to give only two, and some only one period.
As to allowances for sea cadets, they receive no pay. They are given transportation to and from the camps. The sea cadet officers receive pay only while they are under instruction or while they are at the camps. When in the camp the sea cadet receives, of course, board and lodging and medical attention at government expense.
There is some allowance for uniform, is there not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, one-half the cost of the uniform is provided by the government and the other half by, the cadet himself.
I asked also what extra pay the naval commandos get.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am sorry I overlooked that. I have it on a separate sheet of paper here. Naval personnel engaged in combined operations overseas-I think this is what my hon. friend wants- receive when serving at sea the following emoluments in addition to their regular rates of pay: Officers above the rank of sub-lieutenant get one shilling and six pence a day extra, sub-lieutenants one shilling a day extra, and ratings six pence per day extra.
That is the commandos?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. We call them combined operations personnel, but I think commandos describes them.
That is what they call themselves when they write home.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
think so.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
I had another question in regard to civilians working ih administrative offices with naval men and receiving less pay than the naval men.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have looked into that, and if my hon. friend would give me any case he has in mind, even confidentially if he does not want to give the names here, it would simplify matters.
I will do that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Cote) raised the question of the name of the ship Dunver. It is our practice before naming a ship to be very careful to see that the name is not already borne by a British ship or even by a ship of the United States navy, so that there shall not be confusion in receipt of signals by these ships. We found that the British navy had a ship of war called the Verdun. They had no doubt given her that name in honour of the great stand made by the French troops at Verdun in the last war. We therefore could not use the name Verdun and we asked the city of Verdun-I have not the correspondence here, but my recollection is pretty clear-to suggest some other name, and they suggested the name "Dunver", which is an anagram or rearrangement of the letters of the word " Verdun." That name has been criticized in certain newspapers and it has been suggested that we here in Ottawa invented the name because we were unwilling to give the name of the city of Verdun to a ship. There is absolutely no truth in that stoiy. We wanted to honour the city of Verdun, which is one of our larger cities. We are taking the cities now in the order of population. When we found we could not use the name of Verdun we took the name which the city itself decided was the next best name. My hon. friend the member for Verdun wanted to know if we could not incorporate Verdun with other names such as the "City of Verdun" or " La Ville de Verdun." If that can be done we shall do it. The hon. member also spoke of certain resolutions w'hich had been forwarded to him by branches of the Catholic Women's League of Canada protesting against the lack of chapel facilities at certain bases. I have received a great many such resolutions. The building of chapels is going on as fast as I can have it gone on with, but it must proceed I think simultaneously with the building of the other parts of the base. We are doing the best we can in that matter.
Are the chapels to be open to members of any denomination?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes. The three services agreed on a standard type of chapel. In the middle part of it is a reading room, which has folding doors; on one end there is one chapel, and on the other, another; so that each denomination can have the end which is allocated to it, and if it wants more room it can take out those folding doors and have the reading room as well. I am speaking now more of morning services, which I believe some men at a, camp might want to attend and which perhaps they are unable to attend unless a private chapel is provided. For the large services at a big camp on Sundays we do not pretend to be able to build a church adequate to accommodate the men: they will have to hold the services on that day in a drill hall or a gymnasium or something ,of the kind, and it can be done without any great inconvenience. But I am speaking of a place where a chaplain can have an office, where the men can consult him, and where week-day religious services can be held.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) raised the question of naval policy on the Pacific, and the Jellicoe report. I have the Jellicoe report under my hand. It is quite true, as my hon. friend stated, that it recommends the provision of battle cruisers, light cruisers, destroyers and submarines. My hon. friend wanted to know whether we had decided to aim at ships of this type after the war, and generally he inquired what our naval policy on the Pacific was. I may say to my hon. friend that we have not by any means forgotten that this is a two-ocean war, that there is a Pacific ocean, and that that coast has to be guarded. My hon. friend will not misunderstand me, though, when I say that up to the moment in this war it has been necessary for our main work to be done in the Atlantic. That is because we have regarded, as I think the people of Britain do, Germany as the great enemy and we have put our main emphasis on convoy work. I think this is probably not the time to begin to plan exactly the sort of navy we should have after the war. My own feeling is that we should go to work as best we can with the task we have in hand, namely convoy work, which is essentially work for small ships; but undoubtedly, after the war, in the establishment of a Canadian navy, such ships as the Jellicoe report mentions-cruisers and destroyers- should form part of that navy, and for an all-round navy, of course, submarines. But up to the moment in this war, even if we had a strong fleet of submarines manned by well trained men, there would be very little

War Appropriation-Naval Services
for them to do unless we sent them tp far distant theatres such as the Mediterranean or the southwest Pacific. What we need in this war is ships to fight submarines, not submarines themselves.

Does the minister feel that that is the position on the Pacific ocean as well as on the Atlantic? When I mentioned yesterday a policy for the Pacific I was not referring to the period after the war; I meant at the -present time. Is it the opinion of the government that the same type of fleet is needed on the Pacific as we have on the Atlantic, which is in reality an escort fleet?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that there is very little convoy work to be done on the Pacific coast.
It is a question of defending our coast on the Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right; there is a difference right there. Consequently if my hon. friend asks me what the ideal combination would be for the Pacific coast, so far as I can see we should perhaps have to make some changes from the sort of ship we have in the Atlantic. But for the moment we have looked on the Atlantic struggle as our great struggle and we have built the ships which are useful for that purpose. That is not to say that they are not of some use, and of great use too, on the Pacific coast. Then of course in this war, as my hon. friend knows, the association between the British empire and the United States is very close. The fortunes of war have given a certain area more or less to British care and another area more or less to the Americans. We do not overlook that fact when we are disposing of our own navy to what we consider to be the best advantage. I do not know if I am answering my hon. friend exactly, but it is a little difficult for me to give the disposition of the ships, the numbers and the kinds of ships which are here or which are there. I can only tell him that when the war is over, and when plans for what I hope will be a permanent and solidly established Canadian navy are formulated, whoever is here at that time will give full attention, I am sure, to the conditions on the Pacific and to the provision of the proper kinds of ships to meet those conditions.

In effect, then, Canada's
naval policy on the Pacific at the present time is to depend on the United States fleet to protect the west coast? .

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No, I would not want to put it in that way. We have to rely largely on our friends, as on the
Atlantic we have to rely on the great protection of the British fleet. It is true that in this war the British empire is taking a certain area more or less as its own. We have taken the Atlantic, north and south, pretty well, the Mediterranean, and other oceans: the main task of the United States has fallen into other places and it is assuming a great burden there. But I do not quite want to say that we are doing nothing but depending on our United States friends for the defence of the Pacific. We are doing what we can there. We have some ships there still, and they have cooperated with United States ships in expeditions up to the Aleutians, where the Americans have done such signal work in recent weeks. But our main strength undoubtedly is on the Atlantic.

What about
aeroplane carriers for the convoy work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
mentioned in my address that we have that under consideration. One of our officers has been away for some weeks now and will be away some weeks more, in the United States and England, examining the whole question of aircraft carriers, the acquisition of ships, the training of officers and men, the cost and all that sort of thing. I cannot tell my hon. friend anything more definite.

The minister has said that
it will probably be necessary for Canada to have certain capital ships after the war. Is any attempt being made during the war to give Canadian naval men training on capital ships of the British navy? I believe that New Zealand has been carrying on in that way. This would seem to be a splendid opportunity for Canada to get at least some of her men trained on the capital ships and the submarines of the British navy, so that after the war they will be able to man any ships of that type we may acquire.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Nearly fifteen hundred Canadians, officers and men, are now serving with the Royal Navy. Some of them are on capital ships-on battleships and cruisers. Take these men we have now in the high command, like the chief of the naval staff, Admiral Murray at Halifax, or Admiral Jones, vice-chief of the naval staff: these men have served on all sorts of ships of the British navy, including battleships and cruisers, and have had a very wide experience. So that of the fifteen hundred with the British navy, I am sure many must be on capital ships and some on submarines. I know that one Canadian officer is in command of a submarine. I think he is a boy



War Appropriation-Naval Services
from Ottawa. If I mistake not his name is Toller. There may be others. So that they are gaining experience in that way.

Is it a definite policy to
see that some Canadian naval men do get that experience.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. There always has been a flow of Canadian naval officers to the Royal Navy for training, and that has been going on for the last thirty years or more.
I have received some complaints about pay and allowances in connection with some young men drafted from Hamilton. The minister will know something about that-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Too well I know it.

I was asked to inquire as to the treatment of young men who are loaned or transferred to the Royal Navy. One of the complaints made to me was that when they went to the United States they were given no special .pay or allowances to compensate for the difference in exchange as between the two countries. If that is so, I can sympathize with the complaint, because having been to the United States recently, I realize the extent to which prices have advanced in that country, and however much we may be critical of our own price control, when you step across the border you realize that something has been done here to prevent prices from rising. If the situation is as indicated the department should give some consideration to young men who are drafted into the Royal Navy and who then serve out of United States ports or who train on ships of the Royal Navy in United States ports, to see that there is no loss in regard to pay and allowances during the time they are serving there, and that this does not interfere in any way with the possibility of promotion. As I say, I know nothing about these cases and the minister probably does, and I thought that this was an opportune point at which to raise the question of pay and allowances and the question of the standing of young men transferred or loaned, or whatever the term may be, to the Royal Navy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
When a Canadian is loaned to the Royal Navy he continues at his Canadian rate of pay, which is usually higher than the British rate. The particular case to which my hon. friend refers has to do with some men who were in the Canadian navy and who were asked to volunteer for service with the

British navy in combined operations work. Their contention-or rather the contention of a few of them because there are only three men involved out of a much larger number-was that they were not fully informed of the terms and conditions. They thought that they would be with the Canadian navy and would be serving under Canadian officers and as a unit. Twenty-five or fifty of the first detachment felt that they would always remain together but instead they have been broken up into smaller detachments, some having gone overseas. Parents have written complaining that misrepresentations were made, and three of the parents have expressed a very strong desire to have their sons brought back to the Canadian navy on the ground that the conditions were not fairly presented to them. The officers who recruited these men for this service assure me that no representations whatever were made of the kind indicated by the men. It is the old story of one man saying one thing and another saying something else. I hope to be able to straighten out the matter.
As to pay in the United States, that was another source of complaint. They said first that they were not getting any pay for a long time. I had to send an officer to the United States to look into the whole matter and he came back and reported. He did not see these three men because they had gone away. He reported that as far as he could find out there was no justifiable complaint on the question of pay. They were given certain advances in United States funds when they went to the United States. The member for Wentworth (Mr. Corman) had several conversations with me on the point and the whole subject is receiving my best attention.
The member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) wanted to know if there is provision for common law wives, as they are called, in the navy. I think he means dependents' allowance there. The navy up to the moment does not provide dependents' allowance in these cases but an amendment to the Canadian naval regulations is under consideration which will provide some allowance for them, and that has yet to have the approval of the treasury board. As to unmarried mothers, that too will be dealt with shortly on the same basis as it is dealt with in the army.
There were some other questions about Deep Brook, as to whether the establishment there was justified or not. I was asked to explain why this establishment was to cost so much money; why it was required if the 18 R.C.N.V.R. divisions are to be maintained; were other training centres to be closed; would officers be trained there; and, I believe,

War Appropriation-Naval Services
I was also asked to say why it was not established in New Brunswick. Well, there are two things which must be taken into consideration when we speak of training for the Canadian navy. The first is that for many years there were no training establishments in this country in the full sense of the word except perhaps at Halifax and Esquimalt. The result is that the training of nearly all the men required to man our ships has had to be done during war time. We must remember that the Canadian navy is largely a civilian navy enlisted and trained during the war. I may say specifically to my hon. friend that the importance of the 18 R.C.N.V.R. divisions throughout Canada is not affected in any way by the establishment of the school at Deep Brook. Training at these divisions, such as the Brunswicker, Saint John, is elementary training and lasts for a period of from six to eight weeks. It is necessary to acquaint newcomers to the navy with the elementary ideas of life and work in the navy, and I think that work can be done very well at the divisional centres throughout Canada.
There is another thing to be kept in mind. The Canadian navy, up to the present, is a small-ship navy. Most of the actual training for these ships must be done ashore. In this respect our navy is different from navies that have large battleships. Large battleships can carry as many as 250 -men, sometimes, in training aboard, and if anyone has visited a large battleship or a large cruiser he would find attached there a considerable number of young ratings or young officers for training purposes. We cannot do that in our ships. The ships are too small and the accommodation is not there. A large central training establishment is the most economical method of dealing with our problem. The equipment for training is costly and if it were scattered it could not be used to the same advantage. Moreover, it is highly technical equipment and the problem of securing it in these times is a difficult one. There is also another matter to be considered, the shortage of instructors. This is due to the fact that the permanent service was so small for a long period of time that adequate numbers of trained officers were not available for instructional work when the ranks began to grow. Therefore, to concentrate our instructors in a central training establishment means that those available are used in the most economical way. To have civilians in a large training establishment means that they become imbued with the discipline and customs of the navy. They are all lodged and housed by the service, which means a great saving in cost. We pay a man $1.25 a day if he is
72537-222i
living out in civilian quarters and it does not cost us that much when we provide barracks and feed him ourselves. The discipline and health of the men is much better.
Deep Brook is used to requalify officers and men and to provide refresher courses, and therefore it should be as near as possible to the naval bases. Deep Brook answers this problem, without placing the training establishment too close to the main naval base at Halifax, which might not be sound strategically. Of course Halifax is the heart and centre of naval activity in eastern Canada, and has been, as I said the other night, for nearly two hundred years. When draffs coming in from the sea are to be sent for training in gunnery or torpedo work or any other specialist branch, we could not conveniently send them seven or eight or nine hundred miles away. They must be sent to some place not too remote from Halifax, because that is where the ships come in and that is where the drafts come and go.
The training establishment at Deep Brook is not a place where men go to drill. I would point out to my hon. friend that that is one of the great differences between the camp at Debert and the one at Deep Brook. As I understand it, the camp at Debert is purely a drilling camp and the cost was not anything like $5,000,000; I understand it was something like $7,000,000.
I was taking the figures of the Minister of National Defence.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: What are the figures?
He gave them when his estimates were up the other night.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It depends upon what you call cost. I am taking the cost of Debert to include buildings, lands, roads, and other accessories, and on that basis the cost is about $7,000,000. As I say, it is largely a drilling camp and all you need is a parade ground, places for the men to sleep and places for the men to eat. But that is not the case at Deep Brook. In a certain sense Deep Brook is a university where officers and men go to be instructed in very technical work, in things like gunnery, asdic work, navigation, divisional training and so on. These things require a good deal of equipment in order that proper instruction may be given, and it will all be found at Deep Brook.
Would the minister deal with Point Edward now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The hon, member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) stated that he had heard that some of the

War Appropriation-Naval Services
buildings at Point Edward had been erected on filled land and had sagged, in some cases breaking their backs. I instructed the department of works and buildings to call our own representative at Sydney, not the contractor, and he informed them that no such condition exists as was indicated last night. He confirmed what I had seen of the buildings, that the majority of them are not built on filled land. There are one or two, perhaps more, dowm near the wharf which are built on land which is filled to some extent. All that has happened, however, is that one building, a workshop or a machine shop, showed a crack, but it was of such a minor nature that it has not been thought worth while to repair it.
What are the ice conditions there? It is alleged that there is a considerable period during the winter when Sydney harbour is not usable because of the ice.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is a period of time when Sydney harbour is closed to ocean traffic because of ice. The harbour at Louisburg, about twenty miles away, is an all year round harbour.
What about Point Edward?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Point Edward is in Sydney harbour, and the comments I have made about Sydney harbour would apply to Point Edward. As a shipping port it would be closed for perhaps three months every year.
Has Louisburg harbour been reequipped for service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Some ship repair work is being undertaken there, but I do not think any great change has been made.

Has it been fortified?
Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City)I do not think it has in the sense that we speak of fortifying a harbour, but there are guns all around that area. The army is protecting Sydney and all that country, but I would not care to say about naval fortifications, whether we have made any particular defence preparations.
For what purpose is Point Edward to be used, bearing in mind the fact that it is closed to navigation for a certain time in the winter? Will that be Admiral Murray's headquarters?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No; Admiral Murray's headquarters will be at Halifax. As my hon. friend knows, Sydney is quite an important point. I need not go into

all the reasons why it is important, but considering the geography of Canada and the manner in which ocean traffic moves around this country, Sydney has become a most vital point. That is one of the main reasons why buildings are necessary there. There is also a marine slip capable of taking a ship up to the size of a destroyer, and I expect that there will always be some ships in Sydney harbour refitting and repairing. It can also be used to some extent for training, although not to the same degree as Deep Brook.

I want to
commend the minister and the department for having located1 a major naval establishment in the northern part of Nova Scotia where it can give protection to the St. Lawrence route, but I should like to know why preference was not given to Louisburg which is open the year round and is only twenty miles from Sydney. It would appear to me that Louisburg would have advantages over Sydney.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Sydney is a bigger harbour, of course. Louisburg has not a very big harbour.
Still it would be much better than to have a harbour which is closed for several months during the year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The main purpose for which we want Sydney is not affected by the fact'that it is closed by ice. We are concerned with Sydney mainly while there is shipping going up and down that coast; as long as that goes on Sydney is very important. But when the ice comes the pur- . pose for which Sydney is mainly used, in regard to river traffic, disappears.
A great deal of sea traffic passes the year round not far from northern Nova Scotia, even traffic from New York and other United States points as well as Canadian traffic.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
know it passes there, in a general way, but it does not have to use that harbour as we use Sydney in the summer.
I was coming to what the hon. member for Broadview asked in regard to our properties in Toronto. I would tell the hon. member that we have in Toronto five different buildings. There is the Flavelle residence at Queen's Park. That is used by the Wrens and is rented for the sum of S3,000 per year. Then there is a building at 142 Crescent road which is used as the headquarters of the commanding officer of all divisions of the R.C.N.V.R. The rental of that building is $1 per year plus taxes and insurance. Then there is the automotive building in the exhibition grounds,

War Appropriation-Naval Services
which we are given rent free. That is used as the headquarters of the Toronto division of the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has the minister the particulars in regard to the taxes and insurance on the second property he mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: For the Crescent road property the rental is only $1 per year and we pay the taxes and insurance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is what I was inquiring about; how much does that amount to?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not that information, though I can get it. Perhaps my hon. friend knows the property?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is a good property, but I would not say it was a mansion, as it has been called.
What is the rental of the Flavelle property?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is $3,000. Then we have a building at 120 Wellington street, a large storage building, where we lease two whole floors and part of another, at a rental of $9,650. We also have what is. called the Nerlich building at the corner of University avenue and Wellington street. We occupy about five floors in that building for storage and pay $13,000 a year. These are the only buildings we have in the city of Toronto.
Did the minister say $13,000 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, for the Nerlich building.

There was a question which the minister has either forgotten or has not had time to look up. Yesterday I asked if he could give the house some information in reference to the statement made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply as to the extension of the Canadian merchant marine after the war and the part that would be played in that connection by the navy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Frankly I have not had a chance to look into that matter. I .think my hon. friend wanted to know on what basis the merchant marine would be carried on after the war?
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speechtext: Has any survey been made among the men in the navy to see how many of them wish to follow the sea after the war? I believe a survey has been made in the army to find out how many men propose to go farming, and I should think it *would be very useful if the navy knew the approximate number of men who are anxious to go into the merchant marine or to stay with the navy when the war is over.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.

In that event might it not be wise to lay some plans now for training these men. so that those rvho do wish to transfer to the merchant marine after the war will be able to do so? Is the training they receive in the navy sufficient to qualify them to go light- into the merchant marine, without anything further?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is pretty good training, of course, but with all the stress of work we have now I do not think we could begin to undertake to train men for some other service. That would be a little too much to expect. I will say to my hon. friend, however, that we are making a survey of those men in the navy who might want to choose the navy itself as a career after the war; that is under way at the present time. The Canadian navy now has an authorized complement after the war of about eight thousand, I think, and we have not that many in the Royal Canadian Navy -proper, that is the permanent force; we have only about half that number. So that we have caused questions to be distributed at

War Appropriation-Naval Services
the various bases and ports to ascertain how many men at present in the volunteer reserve, let us say, or the naval reserve, might wish to adopt the navy as a career after the war.
Would it not be possible to find out also how many would like to adopt the merchant navy as a career?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, that could be done..

The other evening the minister referred to the divisions of the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, of which he said there were some eighteen. Is one of those divisions located in the province of Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, there is not a division of the R.C.N.V.R. in Nova Scotia.
Why is that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Well, in view of the permanent base at Halifax we have always felt that this took care of the matter so far as Nova Scotia was concerned. My hon. friend, I take it from his language, would favour the establishment of a division there.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I agree with him. I think there should be a division in Nova Scotia; and I hope-I believe-there will be.
Would there be any difficulty in establishing one now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think there would be a little difficulty. Halifax is very much crowded at the present time. As my hon. friend knows, it is very hard to get accommodation there. That would be the logical place for the establishment of a division. I agree that in peacetime it would help matters if there were a division at that point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That will be done.

Some time ago- I mentioned to the minister the matter of purchasing property and constructing buildings for the navy department, and I asked whether this was entirely within the purview of the department. I ask this because similar operations are conducted entirely within the Department of National Defence, for the army, and the Department of Munitions and Supply does most of the work for the air force. I asked further about certain large residences in Winnipeg. Have they been offered to the minister's department for the payment of taxes? These are residences which people thought would be useful for the accommodation of Wrens. Then I asked further about the number of naval officers at headquarters in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We would buy property on the recommendation of the real estate adviser of the Department of National Defence. We would conduct the negotiations in connection with buying the property. If a building were to be erected, it would be done by the Department of Munitions and Supply, at our request. I believe that is the same procedure for all three services.
The three armed services operate in the same -way in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If we wish to erect a building we notify the Department of Munitions and Supply of the kind of building we want, give them the plans, and they call for tenders. That is the way we do it, and the way it is done by the air force, I believe. I think the army does the same, although it may look after some of its own work.
The Minister of National Defence said the other day that they do all their work themselves.

I understood the Minister of National Defence to say they did it all.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Then
perhaps they do.
Who would decide as to the type and cost of building?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That would be decided by the works and buildings branch of the naval services.
Then, there was a suggestion that the department had been offered the use of property in Winnipeg for the accommodation of the Wrens. If the hon. member means that it was offered free, then I must reply that I do not think that is so.
For the payment of taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not know of any such offer, but I shall be [DOT] glad to look into it. Two or perhaps three properties in Winnipeg have been suggested as places where the Wrens might be housed and fed, where they might establish barracks. I do not recall any place offered for taxes. I have not looked into the matter in the last day or so, and I might be wrong about it.
A question was asked as to the number of officers in Ottawa. I had that information with me a moment ago, but it has been' mislaid. I shall give it later.

I should like to ask a question of the minister, but before doing so may I join with other hon. members from the prairies who have called attention to the large number of young men from our part of the country who are in the navy. In view of our great distance from either coast we feel justified in being proud of the type and number of our young men who have joined this service.
My question comes under item 4(a), and relates to the purchase by the Department of National Defence for Naval Services of the property formerly owned by the Winnipeg winter club. I shall remind the minister of some of the facts surrounding the purchase, and I take the facts from sessional paper No. 193 and from Hansard of March 25. The sessional paper was tabled and the answers in Hansard were given in response to questions I had placed on the order paper. We find that this property was purchased last October by the minister's department, and that the price paid was 8256,009, or a little more than a quarter of a million dollars. The assessed value of the property, according to the assessment department of the city of Winnipeg, and confirmed in sessional paper 193, was $94,090. However the portion of that assessment which relates to the buildings is on a basis of
66J per cent of the market value. Accordingly when you adjust that figure so as to arrive at a figure representing 100 per cent of the market value you find that the land and buildings, according to the city of Winnipeg, were worth $129,365.
According to Hansard of March 25, 1943, pages 1536, 1537, 1538 and 1539, the department purchased, in addition to the land and the buildings, all the equipment contained in the buildings. There was a variety of it, and the items are listed on the pages of Hansard I have indicated. The department placed a value of $40,000 on this wide range of equipment.
Then, in addition, according to the information in Hansard, the department made an allowance for fuel, moving expenses, compensation and other incidentals, amounting in all to $8,057.49. These figures I have given- the 100 per cent market value of the land and buildings, the value placed on the equipment contained in the buildings and the item for special allowances-total $177,422.49. The amount paid for the entire property was $256,000. The question which I wish to direct to the minister is, will he explain that difference of $78,577.51? I might point out at once that upon analysis of these figures he will find that the entire difference is between the value placed on the land and buildings by the city of Winnipeg and the value placed on the land and buildings by the Winnipeg winter club, namely, $78,577.51. I could understand it if there had been some sort of compromise between these two evaluations, but with that difference it seems rather hard to explain why the department paid the Winter club's own evaluation 100 per cent.
In the return which was made by sessional paper 193 and in the answers given in Hansard on March 25 it was pointed out by the minister that this price was arrived at after consultation between a member of the Montreal real estate board, members of the Winnipeg real estate board and the real estate adviser of the Department of National Defence. I point out that it does not state that the real estate boards of these cities were in on this evaluation but rather that it was done by private members of these boards. It was also pointed out that a condition of this sale was that the Winnipeg winter club-perhaps I had better read this direct from Hansard-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: What page?
Pages 1539-40 of Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is the second return?

War Appropriation-Naval Services

That is correct. The
first return was not placed on Hansard. As a matter of fact, however, this particular information is given both in the return and in the answers that were placed on Hansard. I will read from pages 1539-40 of Hansard:
It was further agreed that the Winter Club would undertake, to invest the net proceeds of the sales, less the amount necessary to discharge the mortgage and other encumbrances, if any, in victory loan bonds, and would undertake to have such bonds registered in its name; and further would undertake to retain, and not dispose of by sale, at least 50 per cent of the said bonds for the duration of the present war, or for a period of two years, whichever period shall be the lesser, but this condition shall not prevent the pledging or disposal of said bonds for the purpose of securing funds to purchase property or equipment for the establishment of new quarters for the club.
Just on the side, the investing of fifty per cent of the net proceeds in victory bonds, particularly when it was understood that the bonds might be used to secure other funds, hardly seems to me to justify the deal. It might be argued that it has no bearing on it at all. Certainly in my opinion it does not justify it.
I come back to the figures I have already given. The total amount spent in purchasing this property and all this equipment, the allowances for everything which the club listed as on hand at that time, exceeded one-quarter of a million dollars. From the figures which I have given it would seem that the price paid was $78,577.51 more than it should have been. I would appreciate it very much if the minister would answer my question as to why the higher price was paid, particularly when there was such a wide spread between the city's evaluation and the club's evaluation of that property.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not remember all the facts at this time and I have not the papers here, but I recall, as my hon. friend has pointed out, that not only was the chairman of the Winnipeg real estate board-
The return says members.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Perhaps it was the whole board; I do not know. But there was also a prominent real estate man from the city of Montreal and the real estate advisers of our department, and it was their opinion that $256,000 was a fair price. The assessed value of properties of this kind is not in many cases an accurate guide, and I think it would be a very poor guide in the city of Winnipeg. It is difficult for a property of that sort to be sold, as my hon. friend knows. It is not like a house that a man has a chance of disposing of to many people. There are
(Mr. A. L. Macdonald.]
very few people in the market for buildings like the Winnipeg winter club. This was the situation we were faced with. We had a fine naval division in Winnipeg. Winnipeg has always been a strong naval city. We had also there a fine cadet corps, a fine branch of the navy league and a fine naval training base. But these men had no place to eat and no place to sleep except as civilians in restaurants or in homes. We felt that something should be done to improve that condition.
As I said yesterday three years ago this department did not own a single stick of lumber or a single foot of ground between Halifax and Vancouver. We were living entirely in rented buildings and usually in very poor quarters. We felt we should do something and the question was: Will you buy or will you build at Winnipeg? I can tell my hon. friend that if we had started to build a building in Winnipeg to accommodate the division we would not have been able to build it for $256,000. We have now a magnificent building for our purpose. It has a swimming pool. It has a skating-rink surface which can be used for drill purposes on wet days. It has accommodation for sleeping and eating and some recreational facilities. I think we did the right thing in buying that building. As to the price all I can say is that three real estate men and others-I think some prominent businessmen of Winnipeg were also consulted-considered the price not unreasonable. In view of the fact that the building was there and could be had more cheaply than a new building, we felt it was the right thing to take over that building. I can look more closely into the whole correspondence but I do not know that I can ever tell my hon. friend more than that. We acted on the advice of these men, one an outside, disinterested party; the Winnipeg man I am sure was disinterested; and the naval real estate men certainly had only one thought, to get the best price they could for the navy. I am not in a position to say and I do not know that anyone is in a position to say that the price paid was excessive.

I should like to make it clear, in response to the first remarks made in reply to me, that I agree that it was highly desirable to secure proper quarters for this establishment in Winnipeg, and further I agree that these quarters are ideal for the men of this unit. But the question of the ipnce is another matter, and it still seems to me to call for an investigation. The minister has offered to look into it further. I wish to emphasize what I said earlier, that

TFar Appropriation-Naval Services
there is a terrific spread between the valuation placed on this property by the city assessor's department and by the club. As I said before, if there had been a compromise figure in between those two, one would feel a little more confidence as to the price arrived at; one would feel that it had been looked into and all the factors taken into consideration. But when, instead of that, the club's value on its books, 100 per cent- for that is the reply which the minister gave back in March-is paid, I feel that the matter should be looked into further and that the minister ought to make a further statement to the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall be glad to do so at some future date, if my hon. friend will allow me.
The hon. member for Souris asked as to the number of officers in Ottawa. I have now the figures. The total number in one building and another-eight different buildings are devoted to headquarters-is 498.

Does the Canadian navy give any recognition or assistance to sea scout troops? We have heard a great deal about the sea cadets, and I can understand the affiliation between the cadet movement and the department proper. But I feel also that the sea scouts are performing a valuable service. I wonder whether on enlistment there is any report from the navy as to the training these men have received before entering active service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I know my hon. friend is very much interested in the sea scout movement. I cannot give him at this time the number of former sea scouts who have joined the navy; I have no doubt that it is quite large. I believe that some sea scouts go into the sea cadets later on; in that way they come to the navy by three stages. We have not the same close affiliation with the sea scouts that we have, with the sea cadets. I am sure, however, that if the heads of the sea scout movement want to discuss the matter with us we shall be very glad to see whether the association cannot be made somewhat closer.

Yesterday I asked a question as to whether consideration is being given to the establishment of an insurance system. I should like to secure a statement now from the minister in reference to that, and then there are certain other matters under the particular item before the committee which I wish to ask about.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am sorry I forgot that question. The point the
hon, member raises is very interesting, and I shall be glad to look into the system-what is called the American system-which he described yesterday, and to discuss it with my colleagues. Of course any plan of this sort would have to be uniform in the three services. I shall be glad to take it up with the Minister of National Defence and with the Minister of National Defence for Air.

In regard to this item, "construction, purchase, repairs and operating expenses", amounting to approximately $42,800,000, we have as yet very few details other than those connected with the Deep Brook proposition. I would ask the minister to give the committee the capital expenditures which were made in each of the provinces; further, the repairs in each of the provinces, and the rentals paid. I would also ask him in that connection what properties were purchased by the navy during the year other than the one mentioned, in the city of Winnipeg, and the particulars of the rentals. I believe I have already asked for that. Further, would the minister advise whether or not the matter of hospital expenditures is comprised within the ambit of this particular item?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I understand that the matters to which my hon. friend has referred in the main were the subject of a return brought down some time ago on the motion of the hon. member for St. John-Albert. That return should be available somewhere to my hon. friend. There is some difficulty in connection with this return as brought down in the manner asked for- some five hundred man-hours of labour were spent on it-because, when you ask for the amount spent in each province, we do not keep records in that way and it is very difficult to say exactly how much of a certain expenditure is to be charged to Alberta, or British Columbia, or Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick. I have here particulars of the individual bits of land purchased in the east and in the west and elsewhere. Perhaps my hon. friend would look at this return, which I think the hon. member for St. John-Albert also has.

The difficulty is that we have items here of a total of about $44,000,000 and there is not one which we know anything about at all. I have here a return brought down in answer to the hon. member for New Westminster, and the particulars are limited to rentals.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Rentals? Well, no. The return of which I speak, and which was brought down on the motion of the hon. member for St. John-Albert, gives



War Appropriation-Naval Services
rentals, purchases of land, buildings and everything else. I can read over some of the items.
Let us have the major items in the different provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend is now speaking of buildings, is he?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will give some of the larger ones. Starting with Deep Brook, I find the contract price, in round figures, is $8,815,000; the naval ordnance department at Dartmouth, $2,588,000. I am giving now total costs. Some of this work has been already done; some was done two years ago. Then, Nelson barracks, Halifax, $7,324,000; Halifax dockyard, $1,535,000; Shelburne naval base, $1,307,000; Point Edward, the Sydney base, $5,701,000.
Has the minister an estimate of what additional expenditures will be necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: These are contract prices, the full job; the' S5,701,000 is the estimate. Gaspe naval buildings, $732,000; naval service building at Ottawa, $866,000. That has already been spent. That will give my hon. friend an idea. On the west coast there is the Royal Roads naval college, $325,000; Prince Rupert, a certain expansion, $322,000 in one item alone.
They are just the buildings without the land?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: These are the contract prices of the buildings. There are smaller items running all the way down to a few hundred dollars, but that gives some idea of the building problem. I have taken only a few' items.

I should like to have the figures for the total cost at Point Edward. The minister has given the contract price of the buildings, $5,701,000. There are many additional expenditures for equipment, sewage, waterworks, electric lights, wharves and fills. I should like to have a statement of expenditures complete to date, including the cost of the land and the estimated cost of the project completed. If the minister is not able to give it now, he can give it later.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The estimated cost of the buildings, the contractor's figure, is $5,701,000. That is for barracks, stores, canteen and the other work there. Coming to the cost of the land, I have the whole cost here by individual purchases. There are a great many of them and I shall have to

total them up and give them to my hon. friend. It looks as if the land at Point Edward would run to somewhere between $60,000 and $75,000. There are about thirty or forty different lots. I will give the exact figures.
Has the minister the estimated cost of the project completed, including all equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
have the cost of the building but not the cost of such equipment as is necessary.

Including
wharves and fills.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will give all that.
Are the rates of pay and allowances in the Canadian navy the same as those in the British navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Generally speaking, they are higher in the Canadian navy, certainly in the rating class.
In the Canadian navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

When our Canadian officers and: men go to the British navy for training do they get British pay?
Mr.. MACDONALD (Kingston City): I believe I also dealt with that this afternoon. No; they are paid by the Canadian navy at Canadian rates. .

Some of our men went over earlier and joined the British navy in the earlier part of the war. What is done with any requests they make to be returned to the Canadian navy? Is there any way whereby they can get back?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That . is up to the British navy. If they went to Britain and joined the British navy out and out, we have no more control over or business with them.

There is no
comparison then with the air force in this regard. Some Canadians who joined the Royal Air Force are now coming back to the Royal Canadian Air Force. Is there any arrangement whereby the same thing can be effected in the navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is entirely up to the Royal Navy. The men would have to apply to them for permission to transfer to the Canadian navy. We could not transfer them of our own volition.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Is there any way whereby they could go about it? If they wanted to come back to the Canadian navy would they make a request to the Royal Navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The usual thing would be to take it up with the commanding officer. If the man were a rating he would take it up with the captain and, if an officer, he would take it up with his senior officer and indicate that he would like to transfer. Then, I assume, the Royal Navy would ask us, "Do you want this man, or have you a place for him, or are you anxious to get him?" If we were, I suppose the transfer could be arranged.

Would we not rather like to have such a man, who had had that experience? The minister said it was difficult to get instructors. Some of these men might be very valuable back here as instructors in the Canadian navy.'
Is it proposed that there should be any distinguishing mark or badge for officers and men who have served at sea? I have had complaints from men who have had quite a lot of service; they are not exactly complaints, but they express the opinion that there should be some such distinguishing badge to indicate that they have actually served at sea for a certain length of time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Has the hon. member heard complaints from the navy or from other services?

The navy. In the March issue of Boating there are some suggestions from the naval volunteers' association. They appear on page 26.	The minister
probably knows about this. I will not read it, but there are many suggestions which are made by the naval volunteers' association. I suppose this has been brought to his attention. Has it been thoroughly discussed and has any action been taken in connection with it?
To come tq the item we are on at the moment, the minister gave $13,000 for the lease of the building on University avenue and Front street, I believe it is. Can he tell me how many feet of floor space that involves, how much per square foot, whether it includes taxes, and what is the basis of the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The space in the Nerlich building is approximately
32,500	square feet, and . the rental paid is $13,000 per year. Nothing is said about the
taxes, so I assume that they are paid by the owner of the building.
Has the minister seen these recommendations?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think they are from Andrew D. MacLean, but I have received so many letters from that gentleman that I do not remember. However, I will look at the article again.
Does the minister know what the naval volunteers' association is?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have no knowledge of that association, but I imagine it is something in which Andrew D. MacLean is particularly interested. It has no official status and is not connected with the naval department in any way.
Is there any proposal under consideration that men who have served at sea shall be permitted to wear a distinctive badge?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think there is an arrangement now whereby men who go overseas on ships are entitled to wear a badge with "Canada" on it on the sleeves of their uniforms. Beyond that I know of no suggestion to provide any other distinctive mark to those who go overseas. All men in the navy are on active service and are liable for service anywhere.

This afternoon the minister said that plans for buildings were prepared by his department, but I should like to know how many architects or engineers there are in the department and who passes upon the final plans. Some time ago I believe there were two engineers in the department who drew up plans. I understand they were dollar-a-year men and that they left the department because someone else with no knowledge of architecture was put over them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The director of works and buildings is Mr. Young.
Does he pass finally on the plans?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are passed upon finally by the deputy minister and myself. He has a staff under him of roughly fifty architects and engineers, but I can get the exact number later for my hon. friend.
Has the deputy minister any knowledge of architecture or engineering?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
He is a valuable public servant, but his experience has been in business rather than in archi-
3514	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Naval Services
teeture. I have no great knowledge of architecture. What the deputy minister and I would be concerned with would be whether the building under consideration was right as to cost and size and so on. If we wanted a barracks, we would consult the men who were experienced in training men and ask how much space they wanted for a certain number of men. The plans would then be prepared and approved, and the Department of Munitions and Supply would be asked to call for tenders and let the contract.
Does the Department of Munitions and Supply also check on the plans?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, I do not think so. Once it goes from our department, they just act as our agents, so to speak.

I asked the minister a while ago for a computation of the amounts expended in the different provinces. I realize that it would be impossible for him to give this without having a staff in front of him, but I ask that he place this information on Hansard either this evening or to-morrow. I should like the amounts expended in each of the provinces under the various heads.
There is another matter which I did not have an opportunity of bringing to his attention yesterday because I was attending a committee meeting. I refer to the training of probationary officers. I should like a statement as to the number which it is anticipated will be trained this year and what facilities are available for this training. Over the week-end I was in Toronto and met two young men who joined a class of probationary sub-lieutenants last September. At the time I understand there were some sixty in the class. These men are subject to control and direction at all times. They gave up their positions in civil life in order to take this training in Toronto, but for some reason there seemed to be a bottle-neck in the training of these officers and thirty of them are now receiving only a small amount of training. I speak subject to correction, but my information is that they are receiving only two hours a week of training.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot understand why these young men should have given up their civilian jobs.

They expected1 to
be called at any moment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It
looks to me as if these men were attached to the division but had not been called for active service. In that event they should have continued with their civilian tasks until informed

that they were required for full-time service, when, of course, they would have to go. The training of officers is done at King's college at Halifax, and it may be that there is a considerable waiting period for some of these officers who have joined the divisions and are waiting for their official calls. When Deep Brook gets going, some training of officers can be done there arid I believe we shall be able to put them through more rapidly.
