They are down to two hours a week now, but they started off with fairly lengthy training courses.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is something strange about the matter, but I shall look into it.

There are one or two questions which I asked the minister yesterday to which he has not referred. First, I asked about the number of trained men who are serving on shore. The minister said he would have to get that from all over the country and it would take some time; possibly he has not as yet had time to obtain the information. The other question was: How many men have been discharged from the navy on account of wounds; how many on account of injuries; how many on account of illness, and how many on other grounds; and another question was how many Wrens have been discharged from the navy. I do not know whether the minister is in a position now to answer those questions.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, I am, and I must, apologize to my hon. friend for having overlooked them; I endeavour to note down the questions on separate slips of paper. In regard to the first point, it is very difficult to be accurate about this because, as I said, these men are all over the country; but from the information available I estimate that there are about nineteen thousand trained men on shore. Many of these, of course, are at work in dockyards in the maintenance and repair of ships; they are at manning pools; some of them are instructors; some are at signal stations on shore, and so on. I believe nineteen thousand would be an approximate figure. Then my hon. friend asked as to the number of casualties in the navy from wounds. The number of men-wounded is, I think, 159.
Have they all been discharged?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No; I am coming to the number of discharges in a moment. I shall find them directly, but if my hon. friend has any other questions I shall be glad to have them now rather than later on.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Did I understand the minister to say that he would be glad to have any other questions now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, on this item. I thought the hon. member for St. John-Albert had another question on this item.
There was a question I asked in regard to deductions; the minister did not have the information at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am sorry; I do not think I have it yet.
Do I understand that the minister is looking up the answers to the questions I asked?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, I am; I thought I had the information right under my hand, but for the moment it is mislaid. Did my hon. friend have any other questions, while I am looking for this information?

I was going to revert for a moment to the extraordinary expenditure of 812,000,000 at Deep Brook, Annapolis county, Nova Scotia. This afternoon the minister told us that none of the eighteen Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve divisions would be closed up. He did not say, or at least if he did say it I did not hear him, whether or not any of the training schools at those seventeen or eighteen naval bases would be closed, or whether any of the technical schools at the universities would be closed. Will any of the training schools at the naval bases be closed, or will anjr of the technical schools now being operated at the universities be closed? I would also ask the minister to tell us what percentage of the trained men in the navy take refresher courses, and how often those courses are taken. Then yesterday the minister informed us that the decision to build a base &t Deep Brook was reached by the naval authorities. I would ask him when that decision was reached, and also if he would tell us just whom he meant by the naval authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: By that I meant naval officers.
Does he mean the Canadian naval board, or who are the naval authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They would have the ultimate decision, yes.

The minister says they would have the ultimate decision. I thought they were only an advisory board, according to a statement he made in this house in February of this year, when dealing with Commander
Mac-Lean's charges. At that time I think the minister said they were only an advisory board.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is true.
If that is true, how would thej' make the ultimate decision?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If my hon. friend is endeavouring to suggest that I made the decision in connection with Deep Brook, I can tell him at once that I did not make the decision to go to Deep Brook. Naval officers, including the admiral commanding the Atlantic coast and the officers of the works and buildings branch, surveyed up and down the province of Nova Scotia and certain parts of the province of New Brunswick and eventually came to the decision that Deep Brook was the most satisfactory site. They so recommended to naval service headquarters, and their recommendation was approved.
I think the minister will have to admit that the final decision rests with him if this board is only advisory. It is not like the admiralty board in England.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is very much like the admiralty board in England.
It is very much like the admiralty board, but it is quite different from the admiralty board.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: How?

In the statement the minister made last year in reference to the charges made by Commander MacLean, at page 491 of Hansard for February 17, 1943. he said:
In this connection, I should like to observe that the board of admiralty in Britain has no reserve officers on it.
Then he went on:
The Canadian naval board is modelled on the British board of admiralty-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Exactly.
But he went on to say: -with this difference, however, that the board of admiralty is an executive body whereas the Canadian naval board is a body advisory to the minister of naval services.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.
If it is an advisory body to the minister of naval services, is it not up to him as minister to make a final decision?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
In
a matter of this kind, does my hon. friend think I could go all over Newfoundland? He

TTar Appropriation -Naval Services
complained once in the house because I went around the country lecturing too much. He said I should go to Saint John.

He did not
suggest that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My
hon. friend says he did not suggest it. How was I to judge the character of these sites and places, unless I visited them? But even then, would I be in a position to judge, as well as these naval officers? I think not. I did not go up and down the province of Nova Scotia or the province of New Brunswick. In this matter I relied on the opinions of my officers. And I think that having looked at the matter as they did, their choice Was certainly wiser than mine could have been, had I gone over the ground myself.

Yesterday the minister went
on to give reasons why this school or training centre should be established at Deep Brook. He said:
I will say this, that the training facilities in this country are not at all sufficient for the training of our men. Furthermore, even though some men are trained at sea, a great many of them are being brought back for advanced courses:
I do not understand that statement by the minister. It is undoubtedly correct, but if the training facilities that existed last year were sufficient to train officers and men for 150 vessels added to the Canadian navy last year, it seems to me that this expenditure of $12,-"000,000 for a new naval school should have some further explanation than has been given up to the present by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend of course realizes that the navy is much larger than it was a year ago. _ Facilities that might be perfectly adequate in 1940, 1941 or 1942 might be entirely too small in 1943 or 1944.

Well, the minister is going
to add this year to the navy the same type of ships he added last year. Last year he added 150 ships, but he has not said the number to be added this year. Last year he had sufficient training schools to train officers and men for 150 ships. On Monday evening, speaking about facilities, he said:
Our facilities for the training of men have been developed to a point where we are now able to man the ships which are available to us. The task has been difficult, I am bound to say, but we have always been able to keep the manning of ships abreast of construction so that our ships are not kept out of operational duties through lack of trained personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Right.

If the minister was able to keep the trained personnel up to the number of ships being supplied, and if 150 ships were supplied last year, why is it necessary to go out now and spend $12,000,000 for another training centre, in this fourth year of the war? Have the pros and cons of this matter been thoroughly considered? Have they all received his attention?
If the facilities existing last year were not large enough to supply the men who are needed for the ships which will be added this year, was any consideration given to enlarging the training centres which are at present in existence across Canada, and which have cost hundreds of thousands of dollars? Was any consideration given to extending those training centres, or are they now to be abandoned? Or is the minister to keep them up, and also develop this new $12,000,000 training establishment at Deep Brook?
Those are questions concerning which the committee should have further information.
I have one or twro further questions about expenditures at Deep Brook. In addition to information in connection with amounts expended, I should like some further information about buildings to be erected there. How many buildings have been or are to be erected at Deep Brook? What kind of buikL ings are they to be? What will each of them be used for? What is the total estimated cost of those buildings? A return brought down recently showed a figure of $7,775,000.
Then, will the minister give particulars as to furniture and equipment for the establishment at Deep Brook, at an estimated cost of S733.000? Of -what did this furniture consist, and what quantities of each kind are being obtained? What firms are supplying it, and what prices are being paid for the different kinds of furniture beipg supplied?
What was the cost of the' equipment obtained? Of what nature was that equipment? Were tenders called before it was purchased? I would ask, also, to have furnished a detailed break-down of the last item in the return under the heading "other expenditures, $1,294,766". This is a large amount of money, and we are entitled to know how and why it was spent. I ask for these particulars in some detail. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some questions were asked this afternoon about discharges from the navy.
I have here figures showing that from September 1, 1939, to April 30, 1943, there were 1,727 persons discharged from the navy on account of a very long list of physical conditions, and there have also been discharged in the same period four Wrens. A question was also asked as to the number of persons wounded. There were ninety-one wounded and injured who have been discharged.

Mr. Chairman, a year
ago when these estimates were before the house I raised the question of giving consideration to providing housing for the personnel.
I notice, according to information which the minister gave the other day, that there are 20,000 ratings from Ontario, 4,208 from Manitoba, 3,657 from Saskatchewan and 4,436 from Alberta. It is obvious that it will be necessary for these ratings to be away from their permanent homes for the duration of the war. The minister admitted last year that- there were two centres, Halifax and Esquimalt, where there was a very serious shortage of housing. I would draw the attention of the committee to the fact that the United States navy pioneered in the field of war-time housing right from the entry of the United States into the war. It was recognized over there that the providing of houses for as many as possible of the officers and men would make a valuable contribution to the morale of the navy. They admit that it has not been possible to provide housing for all the men who joined, but they have gone a long way toward making it possible for the men to live as nearly normal a life as possible when they were home from the sea. In view of the fact that the minister has found it possible to make commitments for the present year of over . $12,000,000 at Deep Brook, over $2,000,000 at another point, over $7,000,000 at another point, over $1,500,000 at another point, over $1,300,000 at another point, and over $5,700,000 at another point, it seems to me that if we can make such large capital expenditures in the fourth year of the war it should be possible for us to make capital expenditures for the providing of housing for the families of the men who go to sea. I would appreciate it if the minister would state whether he has made recommendations to the Minister of Munitions and Supply with a view to providing housing for the men in the navy, especially at Halifax and Esquimalt.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The question raised by my hon. friend is one that has given a great deal of concern to the three defence ministers. It is not an easy problem to solve. A city such as Halifax is already greatly overcrowded, and the normal peacetime facilities of that city in the way of water mains, restaurants and the like are heavily taxed. It is just a question whether we should endeavour to tax them more heavily still by providing housing for the relatives of service men. I agree that there is an argument on the part of the relatives of the service men who see persons working in factories provided with housing. They may with a good deal of justice say that they are entitled to the same sort of treatment. But up to the present we have not endeavoured to meet that problem. It is a very difficult one.
In reply to a question that was asked this afternoon I would say that there are now some 17,000 members of the Canadian naval service in Canada who are not accommodated in naval barracks. That is one of the reasons why such places as Deep Brook have had to be built. Those 17,000 are being paid $1.25 a day out of which they provide their own lodging and subsistence. It is not the best system, I am bound to say, and as quickly as we can we are endeavouring to provide barracks not only at the coasts but at different points in between where such men can be housed and fed and trained.

Will the minister state whether his officials have visited some of the centres in the United States where the naval authorities have built housing, and whether reports have been received as to the value of these expenditures by the United States government?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think any of our people have visited those centres. I'shall be glad to look into that. I am not sure that the United States government has endeavoured to provide housing for the families of all naval personnel. There is of course in this country always a number of our naval personnel at Halifax and elsewhere who are provided with houses. But to house all personnel and their families in and around bases involves the assumption of a very heavy task.

I did not wish to give the impression that they had provided housing accommodation for all naval personnel in the United States; my understanding was that the United States navy was the first department to recognize the importance of building houses. While I have not been able to get accurate information, I understand

War Appropriation-Naval Services
that they have built betweeu thirty-five and forty thousand units for the families of those men in the United States, and I would appreciate it if the minister would try to get some report from the United States navy as to the value of these projects, and give further consideration to making some similar commitments for the next year, particularly in Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for drawing this to my attention. I shall look into it very shortly.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
5. Personnel supplies and services:	food,
medical and dental stores, clothing and personal equipment, $22,015,072.

Has the minister investigated the possibility of using pocket distillers for supplying water to lifeboats? Pocket distillers are being supplied to lifeboats by the British war transport ministry. The pocket distiller is a compact little machine which makes fresh water of undrinkable salt water. The apparatus weighs forty pounds and costs about $50. It turns out hot water for steaming drinks, as well as drinking water, and uses virtually anything in the way of fuel. In a pinch it will throw smoke signals to a passing ship.
Also, could the minister tell us what arrangements are made to have doctors on our corvettes and other boats, and what position pharmacists have on these ships?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
In answer to my hon. friend's first question, our research units, as I mentioned the other day, have carried on significant experimental work in the matter of life rations for men on rafts and boats. With these rations is a water-can and the water therein is treated in such a way as not to be contaminated by the tin of which the can is made. I cannot say that any conclusions have been reached as to the feasibility of distilling fresh water from salt water, but I shall be glad to look into that.
As to doctors on board ships, the smaller ships\do not have doctors; the larger ones do.
Who looks after the men in the smaller ships? Is that the duty of pharmacists?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There would be a sick berth attendant, at any rate.
That is what I am trying to find out. Is the man in charge a pharmacist?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
He would not necessarily be a druggist. I believe some of them are; but he is a man who has

taken some special training in what you might call nursing and in what we call sick-bay work. He has some skill in treating wounds and that sort of thing.
Does the Canadian dental corps take care of the navy as well as the other services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; the army dental corps.
There is one dental corps for the three services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It takes care of ours and, I believe, the air force also.
Yes, it does.
Does the minister's department allow men who have enlisted or men in training to donate to the Red Cross blood-donor clinics? What arrangements has he made in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I believe that a great many of the men do go. I do not know that we make it compulsory.
Does the department encourage them to go?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The matter is brought before them; the importance of it is emphasized, and they are urged to go, if possible.

I think it must be under this item, namely "personnel services", that the matter of recruiting staffs comes. I would ask the minister whether consideration has been given by his department, as well as by the Department of National Defence and the Department of National Defence for Air, to eliminating the competition which is now carried on between the three services in the matter of recruiting. I believe we all realize that there is a certain pool of volunteers available; it is restricted to young men who have not yet received their call and to those who are within the ages of twenty to thirty-eight and who as yet, too, have not been called, the first being not yet subject to the call, the latter not having yet received the call. A few days ago the hon. member for Parkdale had a return brought down which shows clearly the competition between the armed services today for the same pool of men. According to that return, the Canadian active army maintains throughout Canada 122 recruiting stations with a personnel of ninety-three officers and 548 other ranks; the Royal Canadian Air Force has sixteen recruiting stations located in the principal cities with an administrative

War Appropriation-Naval Services
staff of 140, including specialist staff, seventy-one medical officers, 533 other ranks and fourteen civilians; and the Royal Canadian Navy has twenty recruiting stations with personnel of twenty officers and forty ratings, together with thirty-one Women's Royal Canadian Naval Service officers and ratings. Having regard to the desire and the necessity of conserving man-power, also the effecting of such savings as would come from the concentration of recruiting under one head, has consideration been given by the minister and the other defence ministers to the advisability of eliminating what does appear an unnecessary expense through overlapping and competition?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We do not maintain recruiting stations as such in the sense of setting up separate establishments in separate buildings. What we do have is, at each one of these eighteen divisions and also at other places, a recruiting officer. But in the sense of having a separate recruiting establishment in a separate building, we do not have it. Consequently I do not think there is any great additional expense; in fact there is no additional expense to the navy as a result of the policy we pursue in recruiting.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can give some estimate of cost per man, which is the method we follow in arriving at our total.
I did not ask for estimates of cost per man. I asked for the amount that had been expended under these different headings.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
thought my hon. friend wanted figures to show of what this item was made up this year rather than expenditures for last year.
I am referring to last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My book indicates what the proposed expenditures for this year will be, and we arrive at that by taking-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be glad to get that for the last fiscal year. I understood that we were dealing with the estimates for the coming fiscal year, and that my hon. friend wanted information on that point, which I am prepared to give. If, however, he wants last year's figures I shall have to get them.
Let us have this year's.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Take first the estimated cost of clothing per man. For chief petty officers and petty officers the estimated average cost of a uniform is S1S3, and for seamen the average cost per year is $139.50.
Uniform without equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is clothing and kit such as brushes and that sort of thing, what one might call the personal requirements of the sailor-$183 in one case and $139.50 in the other. For Wrens, the average cost of uniform is $140.17. Multiply that by 5,000, that being the estimated average number of Wrens, and we find the total amount necessary to provide clothing for Wrens. As for sea cadets, $7.50 per uniform for each cadet is the amount. Winter clothing per man is furnished at the average cost of $8.10; that is mitts, heavy caps, jerseys.
Would that include such an item as the bridge coat of sheepskin?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The duffle coat? No. A certain number of these are issued to the ship rather than to individual men.
And they are not included here?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
shall come to that in a moment. These are the main items under clothing. Then we come to victualling stores in the proper sense, such as dishes, knives and so on. Twenty dollars per man is the cost of the things that are

War Appropriation-Naval Services
needed. This includes all the appliances and all the paraphernalia necessary for cooking, such as basins, boards, meat-choppers and the like. The medical stores are estimated to cost 83.58 per man per year. We took the average number of men for the year beginning April 1, 1943, and ending March 31, 1944, which was 70,000, multiplied that item by that number and got the figures which appear in the estimates.

To what extent are members of the fishermen's reserve furnished with supplies? In his statement the other day the minister said nothing about this reserve, and it would be interesting if he would make a short statement as to whether the number of men has been increased or decreased and outlining the work they are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The clothing, victualling supplies and medical necessities furnished to these men would be the same as are furnished to men in the navy.
Are they on full time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Oh, yes, in war time.

What is the number of men
in the reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
think it is something like four hundred, but I am speaking purely from memory and I do not want to put myself definitely on record. This reserve exists only on the Pacific coast and perhaps the hon. member knows more about it than I do.
How many ships?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
would have to look that up.

Were we to cast our
minds back to this day three years ago I think we would all agree that it was the bleakest, the most barren and the blackest day in our history up to that time. Following Dunkirk, June 10 stood out as a tragic hour, the most fateful day in our history. France had fallen, and on this date three years ago Italy declared war against the allies, the most cowardly, the most dishonourable act in the history of the world. Then on that date there was cast a pall of gloom over this city, over the entire country, for three years ago to-day, the Hon. Norman Rogers passed away, killed in the service of his country, than which there can be no more honourable death. The late Hon. Norman Rogers was a gentleman, a kindly, friendly man, a distinguished scholar and one who had rendered conspicuous service to his country.

The Hon. Norman Rogers as Minister of National Defence laid the foundations for the armed forces of this country, the navy, the army and the air force. All agree that in the untimely passing of the late Hon. Norman Rogers Canada lost a distinguished son, one that we could ill afford to lose. However, emerging from the pall of gloom which fell on June 10, 1940, there came a voice that carried inspiration for us as well as sinister portent for the enemy. There emerged a figure, a veritable Gibraltar of democracy, whose indomitable courage electrified his people and galvanized an empire into action. That man was the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, and his was the speech that will stand as the greatest battle-cry of all history. He said:
Come then, let us to the task, to the battle and the toil. Each to our part, each to our station, fill the armies, rule the air, pour out the munitions, strangle the U-boats, sweep the mines, plough the land, build the ships, guard the streets, succour the wounded, uplift the downcast and honour the brave. Let us go forward together in all parts of the empire, in all parts of this island. There is not a week, nor a day, nor an hour to be lost.
Three years have slipped by. With those three years in perspective can it be doubted for a moment that Canada and the Canadian people heard the call? "Fill the armies." Can we doubt that the call was heard after having listened to the magnificent story narrated by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston)? "Rule the air." Can we doubt it when we listened to the magnificent story unfolded by the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power)? "Strangle the U-boats, sweep the mines." Who can doubt that we have heard that call after having listened to the thrilling story told by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald)? "Pour out the munitions." When we think of the continuous flow and tide of munitions that have been turned out by Canada in the last three years, there can be no doubt in anyone's mind that industry heard that call. "Build the ships." There is no doubt that the shipyards and labour of this country heard that call. "Plough the land." When we think of what agriculture has accomplished in the last three years in the growing of grain and foodstuffs, in producing the supplies that have been shipped across the Atlantic, there can be no doubt that the farmer and agriculturist of this country heard that call.
Not only did the Canadian people hear that call, but we in western Canada, the part of Canada farthest removed from the sea, heard that call. In my own city of Regina

War Avpropriatwn-Naval Services
there was established H.M.C.S. The Queen. The naval department fitted out and furnished the winter club and converted it into naval headquarters for Saskatchewan, Out of these quarters located in the most central part of Canada have been turned out over two thousand recruits for the Canadian navy.
Just here I should like to say a word by way of tribute to the men who made that possible, the men who in times of peace with great vision saw to it that in the city of Regina there was maintained the nucleus of a naval company. I think of Lieutenant Commander Hall, the first to command H.M.C.S. The Queen, who now is performing important duties on the Pacific coast. I think of Lieutenant Commander Grant, the second officer to have command, and of Lieutenant Commander Ellison, both of whom are now at naval headquarters here in the city of Ottawa. I think of Lieutenant Commander Pickersgill, who is now in charge of that establishment and who, as a Canadian officer serving in the Royal Navy, spent the last two years on active service, sailing the seven seas, coming back to our midst to perform other important duties. I should like to mention also chief petty officers Jeffries and Smith, who, after all, have had the responsibility for training these two thousand and more recruits who have made such a notable contribution to the defence of our country.
I like to think of his majesty's Canadian ship the corvette Regina, which was christened on October 25, 1941, and which distinguished itself in the Mediterranean when it literally blew an Italian submarine out of the water and captured the entire crew. There have been many references to the policy ^ of the minister in naming corvettes after cities, and the results that have flowed from that policy. At the christening of that boat the citizens of Regina donated four radios and four electric toasters, and the Fidelio club, a group of young girls in the city of Regina, have taken the officers and crew of that boat under their wing and kept them supplied with comforts. I like to think of the action of the department, in naming that ship the Regina, as a tribute to the gallant young men from the city of Regina and the province of Saskatchewan who have enlisted in the Canadian navy.
I like to think, too, of his majesty's Canadian ship the destroyer Saskatchewan. I have taken the naming of that ship as a tribute to the men of western Canada who have enlisted in the Royal Canadian Navy. When the department announced its policy of naming destroyers after leading Canadian rivers, I wrote the minister pointing out that
the Saskatchewan was truly representative of western Canada in that it had its source in the foothills of the Rockies, wended its way right across the province of Alberta and across the province of Saskatchewan into the province of Manitoba, where it empties into lake Winnipeg. So that, in the naming of that destroyer the Saskatchewan, there was paid a tribute to the men of the three western provinces who have enlisted in our navy. I like to think of the action of the department in naming a cargo boat the Regina,* I regard that as a tribute to the farmers and to labour in Saskatchewan. The department and the government have recognized the work done and the foodstuffs produced on our farms, which this boat is destined to carry across the Atlantic to the scene of hostilities.
I am reminded, too, of a passage which I picked out not very long ago, and which no doubt will have a familiar ring:
The British nation can be counted upon to carry through to victory any struggle that it once enters upon, no matter how long such a struggle may last, or however great the sacrifice that may be necessary, or whatever the means that have to be employed.
I do not know of any words that more accurately describe the British point of view or the conduct of the British empire during the last three years. One wonders who uttered that statement. One might think it was Pitt; one might think it was Churchill, or some other great British statesman, but the author of those words was none other than Adolf Hitler, in "Mein ICampf". Twenty-two years ago he accurately appraised the British people; but no doubt on this very night he will regard himself as a greater prophet than warrior.

Again reverting to the duplication in the matter of recruiting, if I understood the minister correctly he stated that he did not feel there was any extra cost incurred by reason of the existence of three distinct recruiting staffs, one for the army, one for the navy and one for the air force. The other day I asked the Minister of National Defence what was the cost during the year 1942-43 of recruiting for the army, and at page 3137 of Hansard the following particulars were given:
Pay and allowances of military personnel, $870,000, of which $510,000 is
chargeable to recruiting	 $510,000
Salaries and wages of civilian personnel	 50,000
Advertising-newspaper, radio, billboards, etc	 375,000
Travelling expenses	 225,000
Miscellaneous - comprising rentals, office expenses, etc., plus costs of special recruiting campaigns not included under above heads	 130,000

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The hon. member has said something about advertising by the armed services. So far as I know there has been no advertising for recruits by the Canadian navy. It is true that sometimes one may see posters on billboards, put up by advertising companies, and advertising certain products. But we have not paid out any money in advertising for recruits.
As I said before, our recruiting officers are stationed at the various divisions throughout Canada, and they do other work in addition to recruiting. They are merely there to attend to the recruits who come in to offer their services. In some instances they are paymaster officers, and in other instances, executive officers. But I would not be willing to admit for a moment that that should be charged up to recruiting. We would have those officers in the division in any event. We simply assign one man whose job it is to look after recruits as they come in; but he has other duties, as well. Consequently I find it difficult to allocate to the cost of recruiting any particular amount in fhese estimates, because, strictly speaking,
I do not think there is any amount chargeable to recruiting.
I do not wish to press unfairly, but to whom is the advertising charged?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is not charged to the navy; I can say that.

Then it must be chargeable to recruiting. Those are the figures I am trying to get. The Minister of National Defence points out, as I said before,' that there are military personnel included in the figure of $510,000, who perform additional duties as well as recruiting. He states that $510,000 of the total salaries of military personnel, amounting to $870,000, is chargeable to recruiting. If the minister will say that he has no information on this, and that he cannot say under what authority or head the advertising is charged-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: What advertising? I do not wish to interrupt, but what is my hon. friend speaking about? Is he talking about advertising for the navy?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I say there is no advertising paid for by the navy; none.
Then I do not know where the ads come from which appear on the billboards. I have, I am sure, seen such ads, with the words, "Join the navy":

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Well, they do not come from the navy. We do not have to do it because, as I have said, we have a waiting list. There are people waiting to get into the navy. It may be that local firms are using pictures of sailors, and that sort of thing, in connection with their advertising. Possibly cigarette firms or victory loan committees are doing something of that kind. But I do not recall any instance where a single cent was authorized to be spent for advertising.
If my hon. friend wishes me to attempt to segregate the recruiting activities in these twenty establishments, as distinct from other duties, I shall try to do so. But it will be extremely difficult, because recruiting forms a very secondary part of their task.
Why do you not advertise?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Because we do not need to advertise.

Then I should like to understand the meaning of the return brought down on June 7. It sets out in detail the fact that the Royal Canadian Navy has twenty recruiting stations, with personnel of twenty officers and forty ratings, plus thirty-one AVomen's Royal Canadian Naval Service voluntary ratings. Is that a mistake? If it is, then I can understand what the minister

War Appropriation-Naval Services
has in mind. But the return brought down only the other day set out in detail the officers both of the navy and of the women's auxiliary who were engaged in recruiting, and it was pointed out that there are twenty recruiting stations.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Those
are the divisions. Those are the men at the divisions, and the divisions would be there in any event. I am sure my hon. friend finds nothing in the return about advertising.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not a word is mentioned about advertising.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend comes down to the matter of recruiting. I say, yes; there are recruiting officers in the navy, who have other duties as well to perform. For instance, in a division such as the one at London, Ontario, a recruiting officer would not be busy all the time in handling recruits coming in. I must add, however, that that city has done very well indeed. It has given some 2,700 or 3,000 men since the beginning of the war, but that would be at the rate of only three or four men a day. That is not enough to keep a recruiting officer busy. Whoever would do that work at the London office would have other duties to perform as well.
If my hon. friend wishes me to attempt to analyse the time spent on recruiting as compared with the time spent on ordinary, naval divisional duties, I shall be glad to do so. But it will have to be general and rather haphazard.
I repeat that no money is spent on advertising, and that recruiting officers in the navy do other work as well. We may have to come to advertising; I do not know. The time may come when we may have to advertise for certain special branches, where we may find a shortage of men. But at the present time no money has been spent by this department for advertising.
I understand the minister to say nothing has been earmarked for recruiting. Has the department a publicity and public relations branch?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes; I gave the details of it the other day.
Mr. ROSS (Souris); In general, or was there a break-down?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
placed on Hansard the number of officers and the number of civilians, with salaries and wages.

In the entire naval department there is nothing set up for recruiting purposes, except these offices. Is the minister's auditing department on the same basis as the auditing branches of the other two defence departments? Who is the chief of the auditing branch, and how long has he been in that office?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The auditor general is, of course, over our department, as he is over the others. He is the chief.
Is there any auditing system organized in each defence department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is a chief treasury officer in the Department of National Defence for Naval Services, who' is appointed by the treasury. He is not our appointee. In addition, we have our own financial superintendent, who is a naval appointee. That is the general set-up.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
6.	Signal and wireless equipment, fine construction, et cetera, $4,592,188.

I should like to have a
break-down of this item. I am referring to the amount of $986,447.64 expended last year. What part of this was spent for signal equipment; what part for wireless equipment; what for line construction, and what for the items included in the term "et cetera"? From whom were these materials purchased? There is an increase of $3,605,740.36 in the item over the amount expended last year. Why is there such an increase?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot give the figures for last year. I am dealing with the estimates for the current year. I shall have to ask my hon. friend to wait until to-morrow or some subsequent day for the information for which he has asked.

What progress has the department been able to make in utilizing or developing devices and appliances to detect the passage of either friendly or hostile ships on the surface or submerged, especially in narrow waters such as the strait of Belle Isle, the strait of Canso and Northumberland strait? There is a belief that at this period of scientific progress we should be able to detect the passage of enemy ships in these narrow waters, and certainly no ship either friendly or hostile should be permitted to move in these narrow waters without a permit. Can the minister give the committee any information on that?

War Appropriation-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It would be excellent if we could prevent hostile ships from moving on our waters simply by denying them a permit, but we cannot do that.

Thit is not fair. I did not suggest that a hostile ship should get a permit. I say that no friendly ship should be allowed to pass through these waters without a permit, and I am asking whether the department is making any use of the latest devices to detect the passage of hostile ships within a certain distance from the shore.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As to our own ships, they do not move in these waters without some sort of permit. There are naval control officers at all the main ports and sub-officers at minor ports. The movement of our own ships is fairly carefully regulated. As to hostile ships and measures to be taken for their detection, I cannot go into that publicly, as my hon. friend will realize, but I can tell him that the matter is under constant investigation by the experts at the British admiralty in London and elsewhere, by the United States naval authorities and by ourselves. Every new device that can be developed to assist in the detection of enemy ships is being studied and developed. Beyond that, I do not think I should go except to say that everybody realizes the importance of the matter raised by my hon. friend and everybody is, I think, working hard on it.

I do not wish to press the minister if he thinks it is not in the public interest to make a statement on the matter. But in narrow waters like the strait of Canso or the strait of Belle Isle it should not be possible for a hostile ship either on the surface or submerged to pass without being detected. I do not press this question for reasons of safety, but I do think that in these narrow waters there should be a certain distance from the shore within which it would be impossible for a hostile vessel to pass without being detected. Can the minister make the positive statement that in the strait of Canso or in the strait of Belle Isle no hostile ship can pass without being detected.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I would ask my hon. friend to remember this. As I have said before to this house, the English channel for some part of its length is only twenty-one miles wide; yet the British with all the strength of their navy and with air coverage from the shores have not been able to deny the English channel completely to enemy ships. That will give my hon. friend an indication of the tremendous difficulties in 
absolutely preventing the passing of a ship even through narrow waters. Not much more than a year ago, as my hon. friend will recall, a German battleship and several smaller German ships sailed through the English channel. That battleship got away in spite of the fact that it was heavily attacked by British warships, aeroplanes and submarines.

Because it
took advantage of the foggy weather.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There was fog when they started out, but the German ships were heavily attacked in the channel and yet they got through. So that the problem of trying to guarantee complete immunity from attack by enemy ships in this place or that place is very great. All I can say to my hon. friend is that in certain waters in the province of Nova Scotia and on the eastern coast there are certain devices and certain protective measures taken, so far as wre can take them, so far as we know enough about them.
Such as listening posts and detectors?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There are various devices which can be used. Beyond that, I do not think I can go.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
7.	Ammunition and bombs, $14,245,890.
How much of this $14,000,000 is paid to the Department of Munitions and Supply? Is any of this money being paid to the British government for bombs?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Part of this money will be paid to the British government. The Department of Munitions and Supply buys all these requirements for us.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I suppose that depth
charges are included in this?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
8.	Armament, including rifles, machine guns, naval guns, et cetera, $42,415,548.
I think the minister should give us a break-down of this. Some of this money will, I imagine, be paid to the British government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Some, yes. I can give my hon. friend the cost for a certain type of ship. Take a destroyer, for example. We estimate that the armament stores would cost $204,300 for the year. We estimate that the armament for a frigate would cost us $187,000.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
That is the new type of ship which is being built?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is a new type of ship. Some of them are built.
I am afraid I have not the exact figures for a corvette; it will be somewhat less than a frigate, probably fifty to sevepty-five per cent.
It is only an estimate, anyhow.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is all.
The minister cannot compute how many days or in how many engagements a frigate or a corvette will be operating during the year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right. All we can do is offer an estimate.
Because if a frigate were in battle for only a week during the year, it would blow away the equivalent of $204,000.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We average it, realizing that some would fight a good deal, some not so much, and some would be laid up for a certain time. That is about as close a's we can strike it as an estimate.
Out of that, how much do you figure you would be paying to the British government?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend that at the moment.
The minister could give me that to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: A good bit of it would come from there. Some of the armament, including certain guns, would be manufactured here; certain others, in Great Britain.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
9.	Fuel cost of ships, $25,257,798.
Has the fuel capacity of corvettes been increased?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The old type corvettes, the hon. member means?
The corvettes and the frigates. Has the fuel capacity been increased on account of the long distance they have to travel?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Of course the new type of frigate has a longer range and a greater fuel capacity than the corvettes.
That is what I was getting at.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I could give my hon. friend some figures concerning costs. The fuel bill is up very greatly, not merely because we have more ships but also because the cost of fuel has advanced very considerably. Take, for instance, destroyers; it is estimated that to fuel them for the year will cost about $5i million. We estimate that fuel for our corvettes will cost more than $7 millions, and for mine-sweepers, over S5 millions.
How many corvettes are in service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know whether I should give exact figures, although perhaps it does not make much difference. There are over seventy and under 100. Fuel for Fairmiles will cost about $900,000.
Of this total amount of $25,257,798, has the minister the amounts expended for oil fuel and for coal fuel respectively?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. There are not very many coal-burning vessels in the navy, and the amount expended for coal fuel is quite small in comparison with the total sum. Destroyers, frigates, corvettes, mine-sweepers and auxiliary cruisers are all oil-burners; Fairmiles are gasoline-burning boats.
While the minister is getting these figures, would he include the costs and quantities of each of the different types of fuel?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not that at hand. I would have to take out the ships which use gasoline and calculate the total accordingly. I am sorry I have not at the moment the total by species of fuel. I know what ships burn gasoline and what burn oil; I could add them together, but it would take some time.
Could the minister give us the total gallonage of each and the cost of each?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will get that. It will take some time.
The minister has not under his hand the exact costs of the coal fuel and the oil fuel. I wonder if we could get that later.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; I will get that.

Has the minister's department explored the possibilities of using powdered coal to a certain extent as an alternative to oil fuel?

War Appropriation-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot say that we have. Our ships are designed, of course, on British models, and naturally we would be guided very much by what is done in England with regard to powdered fuel. I have not heard of any new researches in that field lately.
Would the minister say whether any of the ships newly constructed in Canada or elsewhere are equipped for coal consumption, or are practically all of them oil-fuel burning?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know of any widening of the field in which coal-burning ships are used. In the Canadian navy there are a few relatively small ships which burn coal. As I say, I do not know of any extension of the coalburning type of ship.

Is coal less economical or less convenient, or are there reasons of space which determine the building of entirely oil-burning ships? The reason why I ask is, of course, that we have coal available on our own coast, in Nova Scotia, whereas there is great difficulty in obtaining oil at the present time, for transportation reasons. Are any coal-burning cargo vessels now being constructed in the United States or Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
As
to cargo vessels, I cannot say whether or not any of these are being constructed to burn coal. The whole matter of coal versus oil was thought out in Britain thirty years ago or thereabouts. The old ships of course burned coal. There was a tremendous argument in British naval circles at the time the change was proposed, and the change came before the last war when Mr. Churchill, I think, was First Lord of the Admiralty. At that time, most of the ships changed over to oil for the reason that the range of ships was increased by the substitution of oil. They could carry much more fuel in the same space than if they burned coal. I have never heard of the matter being reopened in England so far as warships are concerned. I have always looked upon the question as having been settled in favour of oil. It must be remembered, of course, that Britain herself has great supplies of coal in England, Wales and Scotland, and her problem of getting oil fuel is much greater than ours because all her oil fuel has to come overseas. So that I should think, if anything could be done to make coal available, either in its ordinary form or in the form suggested 
by the hon. member for Cumberland, namely powdered fuel, none of these possibilities would be overlooked in Britain.

Has the number
of classes of lubricatng oils been reduced? Can the minister tell us that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am sorry, I cannot. I shall have to look into it and get a report on the question.
I know there were seventy-five or eighty classifications of lubricating oil, and at one time they were trying to reduce the number.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have it looked into.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
10.	Acquisition, construction, charter, repair and upkeep of ships, $167,571,202.

I wish to say a
few words about this item, and this is the only time I shall have an opportunity to do so. The other night the member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) used these words:
Sometimes, in this canoe-minded atmosphere of Ottawa, and in the pervading activity of the attitude of the great lakes, which was so completely hypnotized by the pacific influences of the Rush-Bagot treaty of 1817, Ottawa has forgotten that there is such a thing as a Pacific or an Atlantic ocean.
That would seem to be quite a slur on us in the central provinces and on the great lakes. There are a great many ships on the great lakes, and a great deal of shipping goes through the Soo canal; indeed, before the war it was the largest amount of shipping that went through any canal in the world. We have our master mariners and our sailors on the great lakes, and while a great many of them are still today on lake boats, a great many of them are on the ocean, as are also a great many of our lake boats. They are on the routes where the submarines are and these men are risking their lives. I want to pay a tribute to them. A great many of our sailors who are now in the merchant marine risking their lives in that way come from the great lakes, and many of the men in the Royal Navy and in the Royal Canadian Navy have also come from the great lakes. A great many of our men in the Royal Navy and in the Royal Canadian Navy-officers and men -have come from our yacht clubs. There has been a great activity in the city of Toronto for many years in connection with naval cadets, and our yacht clubs have always been

War Appropriation-Naval Services
proud of their affiliations both with the Royal Navy and with the Royal Canadian Navy. A great part of the training of these men was obtained on the great lakes, and we have never exerted any pacific influences on Ottawa with regard to the navy. As a matter of fact, my own city of Toronto has been more navy-minded than any other city in Canada.
I do not know how many men from Toronto are in the Royal Canadian Navy; but, according to the minister's figures, there are 1,722 officers and 20,590 men from the province of Ontario itself. That does not look as if we who are on the great lakes and bordering the great lakes were pacifically minded or had been all these years; had we been, we would not have had that wonderful showing from the province of Ontario.
I take my hat off, and give a great deal of credit, to the officers and men of the navy who are doing such a wonderful job at the present time. Some of them went to the Royal Navy because they could not get into the Royal Canadian Navy at the beginning of the war, and I pay tribute to them for their valour and gallantry in the performance of their duty. I wish to put that on record lest I should be misunderstood. I have no criticism to make of the men of the Royal Canadian Navy or the naval volunteer reserve or the naval reserve. As I say, they are doing a wonderful job under very difficult circumstances. Their job is not a showy one; they are plugging away day in and day out. I know a great many of them and I know the difficulties they have to face. Some have been doing good work as far away as the Mediterranean. They have been through the "shows" over there, but they do not get the glory that some of the other forces do.
I do not think there is as yet any ship in the navy named after either my own province or my own city, and I suggest that when we get one of the new and bigger destroyers we might have it called the Toronto.
Could the minister say in a few words what the functions of the various types of ships are? It is not very well understood what the functions of the Fairmile or the corvette are; what a frigate has to do; what is a destroyer, and so on with regard to other ships we may have. A resume on that question would be interesting. I do not know whether the minister can tell us what the range is or how far they can go and how they are armed, or the number of each classification of ships we have in the navy. There is great misunderstanding on the part of a good many people as to the functions of these various ships.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Before I discuss my hon. friend's remarks, somebody asked about the total amount of fuel consumption. I have here the total amount estimated for the year. For bunker in barrels we estimate that we need 5,694,000 barrels; for diesel fuel in barrels we estimate 227,000 barrels; and for gasoline in gallons we estimate 5,336,000 gallons. These are the figures which were asked for by the hon. member for St. Paul's and which I could not put my hand on at the moment.
What was the cost of each item?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The estimated cost of bunker oil is $4.44 a barrel; of diesel oil, $4.66 a barrel; of ordinary gasoline, 27-93 cents a gallon; of high octane gasoline, 32-04 cents a gallon.
What were the tonnage and cost of coal fuel used?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I cannot lay my hands on that figure, but I will get it for my hon. friend. It is a small item. I am not sure whether it is 1,000 or 10,000 tons. I know I looked it up some time ago and was rather surprised that it was so low.
I can say to the hon. member for St. Paul's that I hope we shall be able to call a ship of the Canadian navy after his great city. We have adopted the policy of naming destroyers after Indian tribes or rivers, and we do not wish to break away from that practice. It is a simple and convenient way of naming ships, to name them after a river or a tribe or a town, or after a flower as is sometimes done in Great Britain.
You might name our first cruiser after Toronto.
When an application is made to name a ship after a town or city, how is it dealt with and in what way is the final decision arrived at?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Years ago when we began to use the names of towns for corvettes we began in a rather unscientific manner and took names as they occurred to us, some of them being of towns that were quite small. As the navy expanded we began to see that we would have to systematize this practice, and for some time we have been using the towns and cities in order of population.
Are there any counties that have been honoured in this way?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
There are one or two. The city of Cornwall asked

War Appropriation-Naval Services
to have a ship named after that place, but there is already a famous ship in the British navy called the Cornwall. The citizens of Cornwall stated that they would be glad to have a ship named after the county of Stormont, and consequently that name was given to a ship. Yes; we can consider the names of counties.

I believe an application was made at one time by my own county. In the first victory loan Haldimand was the first county to go over the top, and the people asked that the county should be honoured by naming a vessel after it. I do not know just what was done, but the request was never acceded to.
Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City) r I shall give consideration to what my hon. friend has said.
My hon. friend from Toronto inquired about the uses to which these ships are put. Shortly after the outbreak of the war the auxiliary cruisers, of which we have three, were converted to their present uses. Their range is considerable, one of them having made a trip to Hong Kong and back to Vancouver. They do escort work, guarding unarmed merchant ships, and carrying out other duties which may be assigned to them. I think everybody knows that destroyers are so named because they were first built to destroy U-boats. That is still their chief purpose. They carry torpedoes, and apart from some motor craft are probably the fastest type of warship afloat. They are very useful in providing a screen for the larger ships and are used to protect ships in convoy.
They have considerable fire power.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The corvette was designed mainly for escort duty with the convoys. It is built somewhat on the lines of the whaling ship. Corvettes can be turned out relatively easily for a ship of war, and they have done excellent work in this war. If it had not been for these little ships, the situation might be very different for us to-day. It takes about as much time to build a destroyer either in Great Britain or here, as it does to build three corvettes. They can be built on the lakes and taken down to the ocean through our canals and rivers, something which could not be done with a destroyer. We were fortunate in having started to build these ships early in the war. We have more than seventy of them in our navy, and we have built a great many for the navy

of Great Britain. Then the frigate I would classify as being in between the corvette and the destroyer.
We have not any of them yet?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Some of them are afloat, but they are just coming into use. Generally speaking, they serve the same purpose as the corvette. They have more speed and a greater range than a corvette. They are larger and have more accommodation for the crew, which is larger than that on a. corvette.
Is it expected that the frigates will take the place of the corvettes?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I think we shall always have corvettes.
Mr. DOUGLAS (Weyburn); Has the frigate heavier fire power?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: About the same, so far as guns are concerned. The corvette is not to be trifled with because it has good hitting power. It lacks the speed of the destroyers or the larger ships. The frigate is about the same as the corvette in fire power; it has more guns, but they are of about the same strength.
Is it as good a sea boat as the corvette?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is said to be better. Those who have tried them are very much delighted with the frigates, which are said to be splendid in every way.
Could the minister tell the committee the speed of the corvette as compared with that of the submarine?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I think about the greatest speed a submarine can make on the surface, so far as we know, is about nineteen or twenty knots. It is difficult to estimate these things accurately, I suppose, because actions of this kind are carried through so rapidly. When a submarine submerges, however, its speed is cut down to less than half the surface speed; I think about eight knots is the best it can do under water. A corvette can easily deal with a submarine when it is submerged, but on the surface it would be desirable if the corvette had a little more speed; I will put it in that way. The frigate supplies that need and is consequently a welcome addition to the fleet.
The mine-sweepers are, of course, intended to sweep up and destroy mines laid by the

War Appropriation-Naval Services
enemy in our waters. As a matter of fact, we have used a great many of these minesweepers in the same way as corvettes, and in many respects they are the same sort of ship. They have guns; they have depth charges; they have asdics and so on.
Have we about enough mine-sweepers now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
We have a good fleet of mine-sweepers. Fortunately we have not been bothered very much by enemy mines, but we are ready to deal with them if they do show up in our waters.
Then I pass on to the Fairmile, which is a wooden ship with a fairly good turn of speed, but of course without the endurance or the strength or the seagoing qualities of the corvette. In its present form at any rate the Fairmile will never be a transatlantic escort ship. It is very useful in coastal waters, such as the Irish sea or the English channel or the Bristol channel, and on this side it is useful in such waters as the river and gulf of St. Lawrence, and thereabouts.
Then w'e have the fishermen's reserve, about which my hon. friend asked previously. I have counted up the number here, and I think we have about fifty fishermen's reserve boats. In addition, of course, we have a great many other harbour craft, which are not fighting ships at all, such as tugs, some tankers, and gate vessels, which are used at the gates which guard the entrance to certain of our harbours, where there are nets stretched across which can be opened and shut at will. These gate vessels attend to that work. There are a great many of these other ships, which I do not think I need mefition particularly, but which in their own way are all useful.
The Fairmile is not really a fighting ship, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, it can fight; it has the means.

That is what I do not quite understand. Is it not more of a reconnaissance ship? It has no torpedo tubes, like the British ship of' the same sort, and it has not much fire power. Of course it has depth charges-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

-and I suppose its speed would make up for whatever it might lack in dealing with a submarine, but I was wondering if it was really a fighting ship.
Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City) ; Yes; it has depth charges and guns, but it is a
wooden ship and it is not extremely powerful. It has more speed than a corvette but, as I say, it is mainly useful in coastal patrols and narrow waters, such as the gulf and river St. Lawrence.

Is it customary, when ships are sunk, to give the same names to n'ew ships? I ask this because the minister mentioned the practice of naming some of these ships after cities across Canada. The town of Weyburn was greatly honoured by having a corvette named after it, and the citizens of that town took great interest in the welfare of the officers and men of that ship. We sent radios for the entertainment of the men, and the women of the town supplied them with comforts and kept in contact with the crew. Naturally we felt very badly about the loss of the ship, and we are hoping that at some future date there will be another Weyburn and that the citizens will be allowed to take the same interest in the welfare of that ship. I wondered if there was any tradition in the navy against that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, not if the ship has been lost in action; we consider it quite a good thing to give the same name to another ship. If it has been lost through a marine disaster, a collision or something of the kind, it is not considered lucky to use that name again, at least for some time. But when a ship has gone down fighting, as the Weyburn did, I am sure it would be an honour to the navy to have another ship of that name, and in due time we shall have another Weyburn. I do not know whether any ship is available now; it may be some months, but we , have not forgotten the Weyburn. A ship called the Charlottetown was lost in action last year; this year we have given that name to another ship. So it is with the destroyer Ottawa, which went down fighting while protecting a convoy last summer. We have given that name to one of the destroyers lately received from Britain.

On behalf of my constituents in the riding of Halton I should not like these naval items to pass without saying a word of appreciation and congratulation to the minister, the officials of his department, and the officers of the navy in regard to the tremendous expansion that has taken place in Canada's navy. We in Halton are rather navy-minded, since we were so fortunate as to have two of these little ships named after towns in the riding, the Burlington and the Oakville, and the minister and the admiral of the fleet were so gracious as to come to the riding for the christening

War Appropriation-Naval Services
of these vessels. So that it is only natural that the people of Halton should be very
navy-minded.
On looking over the record, I cannot help but be very proud of my native province of Ontario in this connection. The hon. member for St. Paul's has referred to this matter already this evening, but I know he will not mind if I say something about it also. Our little navy, at the opening of the war, had just fifteen small ships and a personnel of fewer than two thousand. As we know, it has grown until now it has something over 550 ships and a personnel amounting to two-thirds the peace-time establishment of the British navy. The story is almost unbelievable. and would not have been possible but for the very best and .most efficient management and direction on the part of the minister's office and the permanent naval force, as well as the greatest of cooperation on the part of the civilians of this country.
I should like to put on record a few items of particular interest to Ontario. Though a land-locked province, except for the waterways of the St. Lawrence, Ontario has contributed nearly forty per cent of the manpower of the Canadian navy as it stands to-day, and has built just over one-half of the ships of that navy. Within Ontario there are seven reserve divisions of the Royal Canadian Navy. These divisions are the recruiting and basic training establishments of the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve. They are situated at the following centres: Hamilton, H.M.C.S. Star; Kingston. H.M.C.S. Cataraqui; London, H.M.C.S. Prevost; Ottawa, H.M.C.S. Carleton; Port Arthur, H.M.C.S. Griffon; Toronto, H.M.C.S. York; and Windsor, H.M.C.S. Hunter. Depending upon the area and population which they serve, these Ontario training establishments vary in. size. H.M.C.S. York, at Toronto. witli a complement sometimes as high as 1.800, is the largest inland training base in Canada, and one of the largest in the entire British Empire.
These seven divisions, as are all R.C.N.V.R. divisions in Canada, are under the command of Captain E. R. Brock, R.C.N.V .R., commanding officer, reserve divisions.
H.M.C.S. Conestoga at Galt, Ontario, has the distinction of being the only ship in the Royal Canadian Navy manned entirely by women. It is the W.R.C.N.S. basic training centre, with a complement approaching the 600 mark.
So that hon. members can fully appreciate how thrilled the people in my constituency were when, less than a year after the minister and the admiral visited Oakville for the

christening of the ship Oakville, we read in the press that the Oakville had made her first kill. In the middle of the night the corvette Oakville had rammed a German submarine three times, and on the third occasion had made a really good job of it. The crew were taking no chances, and a boarding party of two, in the diark of night, jumped from the Oakville aboard the submarine, and bumped off three men on the deck. One man went below to take care of the German crew.
One of them was a Brockville boy.	.

Quite true. Checking over the crew of'the Oakville, it would seem that it was the Oakville only in name. Men were there from all parts of Canada.
At the outbreak of war our naval officers had a rather serious choice to make. There were three types of navy to choose. One was a navy of capital ships, the second a navy of submarines, and the third a navy for convoy duty. Fortunately for Canada I believe-and I believe the house believes-the correct choice was made. Canada decided we would specialize in convoy work. Look at the result to-day. To-day the Canadian navy is doing half the convoy duty on the Atlantic ocean, and has safely convoyed something over 13,000 vessels, with a loss of less than one per cent. A Canadian naval officer and a Canadian air officer have complete operational command over the entire western half of the Atlantic. Therefore I wish to add my word of congratulations and appreciation with respect to the tremendous task which has been so well carried out.
Just one word in closing. It is difficult for us to appreciate the size of the Canadian navy. Looking over figures which might make a comparison possible I happened to find this:	Do hon. members know that in this
year of this war we are spending on the Canadian navy an amount greater than Canada's total expenditures during the peak year of the 'great war?

In the course of his statement on Monday night about the work of his department and the activities of the Canadian navy, the minister said, as reported at page 3406 of Hansard:
To-day the Canadian navy boasts a fleet of over 550 ships of all types.
That statement must have been carefully prepared. I believe it was given fairly wide publicity in the press. I regret to say it was not correct, and upon reflection I think the minister will agree with me that it was not

War Appropriation-Naval Services
correct. I think the record should be kept straight, and the size of our navy should be kept in its proper perspective. We get nowhere by boasting.
We have no capital ships. We have no ships of many other large classes. The minister was much nearer the mark, and much more accurate this afternoon when he said that our navy is a small-ship navy. With that statement I find no fault. But the statement he made on Monday evening should be corrected.
How many of the 550 ships, or thereabouts, in our navy are manned by over 100 men? How many have establishments of over fifty men? How many are manned by over twenty-five officers and men? If we have seventeen destroyers-and I do not know the exact number-and if each destroyer has a crew of 160-and that is about the establishment of a destroyer; it may be a little more or less- then we would have 2,720 men on our destroyers. If we have 120 corvettes-and I do not know the exact number-and the establishment of a corvette is fifty-eight men, then we would have 6,960 men on our corvettes. This accounts for 9,680 men out of the 20,000 men in our navy who are at sea. Then, of that 20,000 we have 1,400 in the British navy. The remainder of men at sea would be about 8,920, and they would be distributed among 413 ships, or an average of about twenty-one officers and men to a vessel.
Vessels of this size cannot be described or regarded as very large - fighting ships. Last May when the minister's estimates were before the house he told us we had about seventy-five corvettes, about forty-five mine-sweepers, about a dozen armed yachts, about two dozen Fairmiles and between twelve and twenty destroyers in the navy.
