Would he tell us how many destroyers, corvettes, mine-sweepers and Fairmiles we have in the navy to-day? Have improvements been made in the corvettes? How many Fairmiles are in commission? Of those in commission how many, on an average, are on active service, and how many laid up for repairs? Is it the intention of his department to increase the number of Fairmiles? Have they given satisfaction?
The break-down that he furnished us with states that $74,979,157.67 was spent for the acquisition, construction, repair and upkeep of ships during the past fiscal year. This year the estimated expenditure is $167,571,202. That is an increase of over 100 per cent. I would ask the minister if this means that the number of ships which were taken into the navy last year, namely about 150, is to be doubled, or does it mean that different and
more expensive ships are to be built? I would also ask the minister if there are many ships under charter by his department, and whether he can tell us the approximate number under charter and just what kind of ships they are and the nature of their charter parties.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: First of all I would ask my hon. friend, in what respect does he allege that my statement as to the Canadian navy consisting of 550 ships of all classes is not correct?

I state that you cannot say you have a navy of all classes when you have no battleships, when you have no first-class, no second-class and no third-class cruisers, when you have no submarines, when you have no aircraft carriers and when you lack several other types of ships which are found in any of the great navies of the world.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: When I speak of a navy of 550 ships of all classes what I mean is, not that we have every type of ship in our navy,. but that 550 is the total number of ships of all kinds, great and small, that we have. That is what I mean, and I think my hon. friend might once in a while give the benefit of the doubt to this department, and not constantly put the most unfavourable possible construction on what is said or done.

I am sure we all admit that the Canadian navy has made wonderful strides and that a great deal of credit is due to Canada and to the department for what has been accomplished. While sitting here I have been listening to a number of members doing a little boasting about the corvettes and other ships named after their towns or districts. The hon. member for Regina gave quite an oration to-night along that line and we listened to another just a few moments ago. I did not intend to take any part in this debate, but after what other members have said I feel impelled, to speak of my town and the province of Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan itself has a splendid record so.far as the navy is concerned, because out of the total navy personnel of 59,000 officers and ratings that province has contributed 3,787, and we shall contribute a great many more officers because I am sure that those who are now undergoing instruction will acquit themselves creditably.
My own district and in particular the town in which I reside have a splendid record. A great number of our boys have joined the navy, and I should like to mention in particular two boys from my town, Garden and Cooke, one of whom has distinguished himself by working his way up until he is now

War Appropriation-Naval Services
second in command on one of the corvettes. His name is Grant Garden. The other boy from my town, Leighton Cooke, is in the medical service in the navy, serving as one of the chief officers on a hospital ship which has sailed on the Atlantic and which at last reports was in the Mediterranean. I wish that to go on the record here, and if there are to be any more ships named after certain districts or towns I think the Minister of Agriculture will join with me in suggesting that Qu'Appelle be given to a corvette or some other naval vessel. It is a historic name in our province. Fort Qu'Appelle was an important fort in the days of the early settlement of our province and in the northwest rebellion. So that I suggest to the minister that the name Qu'Appelle be given to one of our new corvettes.
I asked the minister a number of questions a few minutes ago about the establishments on the ships in the Canadian navy. Could he furnish me with an answer to those questions this evening?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend wants to know the number of men in the crew on each type of ship; is that it?

No. My question was this: How many of the 550 ships or thereabouts in our navy are manned by crews of over 100 men; how many have an establishment of over fifty men; how many have an establishment of over twenty-five men?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know that I can give my hon. friend the exact number of ships, but I can tell him that all destroyers would have a crew of over 100 men, and frigates also. Corvettes and minesweepers would all have crews of more than fifty men. The usual crew of a Fairmile would be less than twenty-five. I do not think I can give publicly the exact number of destroyers, corvettes, mine-sweepers or any other class of fighting ship that we have, I have never given that. I have always stated that we have something like 500. That is as near as I can give it. Our auxiliary cruisers would have a complement of something over 200.

I also called the minister's attention to the fact that last year when his estimates were before the house he gave us in round figures, and I presume they were approximately correct, the number of destroyers, the number of corvettes, the number of yachts, the number of Fairmiles, and I think some other types of vessels in the Canadian navy. I wonder if it is not possible for the minister to give us to-night in round figures

similar information, in view of the fact that the navy has increased by about 150 ships during the past year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend exact figures. To be very general, the number of destroyers is more than twelve and not quite two dozen. As I told the hon. member for Cumberland, we have over seventy corvettes in commission at the moment. We have nearly as many mine-sweepers as corvettes, and about an equal number of motor launches of one kind and another. We have also various patrol craft and auxiliary vessels-harbour patrol craft, fishermen's reserve vessels, and the like- making up the rest of the navy.

Is the minister satisfied with the position in escort vessels? Last February a statement was made by Desmond A. Clarke, director general of shipbuilding, that it was most important that we should get more men to work building these escort ships. He estimated the number of men required as "in the thousands"-
"And we need them right now, not for cargo ships but for fighting escort vessels," he said. "We must lick the submarine. There is no use building more cargo ships to have them sunk."
That was in February, and I understand that considerable progress has since been made in getting additional escort vessels. But what is the situation at the present time? Is Canada building sufficient escort vessels to give the navy a reasonable chance to do its job?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is difficult to say whether we have enough escort vessels. We could use more, of course; so could every navy in the world, I suppose, if it had the men to man them. I can only say that we have tried to keep reasonable accord between our training of men and our production of ships. We are getting just about as many ships as we can comfortably man.
The minister is satisfied, then, with the production of escort vessels in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
So far, on the whole, yes. There have been occasional disappointments; there have been delays, and many of them are unavoidable. Take the procurement of machinery; it is very difficult to get all the machinery for these ships on time. Much of it is delicate and intricate; some of it has to be obtained from factories outside this country, and all ^ sorts of things may occur to delay the furnishing of materials, but these are disappointments which one has to expect. On the whole I am not dissatisfied.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Not long since, the First Lord of the Admiralty of Great Britain, speaking in the House of Commons, I think on his own estimates, said that this country had made remarkable progress in shipbuilding, considering what it began from before the war. My hon. friend knows that the shipyards in the west and on the east coast were practically idle. I do not suppose that the tonnage built in Canada before the war, say in 1938 and 1939, would amount to more than a few thousand tons a year. Now it is well over a million tons, including cargo and naval ships. Mr. Alexander was happy and generous enough to pay a deserved tribute to what had been done.
The minister is satisfied with the production of escort vessels in Canada now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: On the whole, yes.

What progress has been made in the production of destroyers? We commenced some time ago. How is the work progressing? There were newspaper dispatches in March of this year to the effect that there was difficulty in getting some of the equipment from the British manufacturers, that is, some of the data, that they were holding out on information which was necessary in order to proceed with the construction of these ships. If that was so, it was a serious situation. Would the minister tell us the position at the present time, and would he also let us know whether more destroyers are to be built in Canada, and whether this work is being carried on in such a way that it will be possible for us to build destroyers after the war in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend raised the question about the supply of machinery and materials from Great Britain. Statements were made, I am sure in all good faith, that the British manufacturers were not willing to part with their plans for machinery. I think that arose over an act of the British censor, in stopping some plans which were being sent out from Britain to a shipbuilding firm which is building destroyers in Halifax. The British censor, acting I have no doubt under the censorship regulations, returned these plans and said he would not let them pass through to this country. That delayed for some months the securing of these plans, and it was supposed by some that British manufacturers were holding them up, when as a matter of fact the delay was caused by the British censor. I am glad my hon. friend brought that matter up, because I wish to do justice to the British manufacturers and not have it thought that
they deliberately withheld plans in order to concentrate all shipbuilding construction in their own country. That was not the situation. On the other hand, I understand how the people in Halifax would feel. Not being able to explain this delay, knowing the plans should be there, and not finding them there, they would assume that there was some deliberate policy of selfishness behind it. So much for that.

What about the rest of my questions, namely the progress which is being made in the construction of these destroyers, whether more are to be built in Canada, and whether it will be possible for Canada to build destroyers after the war?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
We have two destroyers building in Britain, very near completion. I hope they will be completed within a couplr of months. In addition, we have two building in Canada. My hon. friend asks as to the progress made on these two. It is on the whole satisfactory, considering that this is the first job of the kind. Again, we are finding some difficulty about getting the machinery'in on time, but we are endeavouring to speed it up. We hope to get the ships out not too far away from the contemplated completion date.
As to whether we in Canada will continue to build destroyers after the war, if there is a Canadian navy, as I hope there will be, destroyers will form part of it, and there is no reason why they cannot be built in Canada, particularly in peace time. There will not be nearly as much trouble about getting skilled help from Great Britain in peace time if we need it, as there is today. It is very difficult to get skilled shipbuilders out of Britain now because they need them all there. After the war that condition will not apply to nearly as great an extent as it does now and consequently there will not be the same obstacle to the building of destroyers in this country. The construction will cost more, probably, than if they were built in Britain; otherwise there is no reason why we could not train skilled shipbuilders here to do the work and do it well.
Would we be able also to build light cruisers in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes; I think a cruiser would be easier to build than a destroyer, which is one of the most difficult of all warships to build on account of its tremendous hitting power and strength contained in a very narrow space. If you can build a destroyer, I think you can easily build a cruiser.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

Early this year Nelson, in the eastern portion of British Columbia, through the board of trade of that city, submitted to the .minister's office blueprints and specifications and the fullest details of the community centre in which the city has invested $300,000. It asked the minister if he would not give consideration to the use of the civic centre for the purposes of a naval training school. There are recreation grounds and there are ample facilities in this community centre. There is ample accommodation for the purposes of residence, and the city of Nelson has contributed generously in men to the three arms of the services. It has responded most creditably to the six loans. But it has not had recognition of any kind whatsoever from the government in the way of war industries or the establishment of any war service.
I want to ask the minister if in all fairness he will not give consideration to the request of the city of Nelson. Will he not look into these plans. We have there not only accommodation in the civic centre but about 100 miles of waterfront including Kootenay lake, which offers the most acceptable facilities for naval training. Perhaps the minister in a moment of generosity will give consideration to the request from that city.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend and I certainly will give consideration to his request. I remember very well the letter from the board of trade. The best I have been able to do is to give the name of Kootenay to one of the destroyers, and while that is not a material advantage to the people, it is some recognition. I shall keep fully in mind the possibilities of Nelson, and again I thank my hon. friend for having drawn the matter once more to my attention.
How does a minesweeper compare with a corvette in cost? Are they not about the same price?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Cost?
Yes; cost of production.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The larger mine-swee.pers cost more than corvettes. There are various grades of mine-sweepers. The larger ones are more expensive than the ordinary type of corvette, and then you grade down to the smaller ones, which are about the same as the corvette, while there are some others not so expensive as the corvette. They run in various sizes.

I have in mind the larger mine-sweepers which cost more than the

corvettes, and I was wondering if they were continuing to make these vessels. Has the corvette not proved better as far as convoy work is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
think they are both needed; both have their uses. We have more corvettes than minesweepers, it is true, but the difference is not very great, and we are continuing to build both.

The mine-sweeper
has not the same range as the corvette. Is that not one of the difficulties?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Usually that would be true. It depends on the type of mine-sweeper the hon. member has in mind. The corvette has a little more than some of the mine-sweepers. 'There are several grades of mine-sweepers. Generally speaking, the corvettes have greater endurance, but some of the mine-sweepers come up fairly close to them-the larger type.
What is the tonnage of the corvette and the tonnage of the Fairmile? Can the minister give some idea of the tonnage of the smaller craft that are fitted for the many duties of modern sea warfare?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not quite see the point of the question and I am not sure whether it should be answered. I do not see the point of asking for the tonnage of corvettes and making such things public. We do not usually do it.
I will not press for it if the minister does not think it should be answered.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend privately what it is for the various types of mine-sweepers, but I am inclined to think we should not make it public. We have never given to the public the exact dimensions of ships, and I do not think I should do so.

There is just a word I should like to say. At the moment I happen to be the only one of the Winnipeg members in the house, and so I feel I would be remiss in my duty if I did not join with others who have expressed pleasure at the honour conferred on various cities and towns in the names given recently to Canadian ships of war. The people of Winnipeg are quite honoured in the decision made to name a ship after our city, and already considerable interest is being taken in this ship, as will be taken in the crew. Perhaps the committee might enjoy a bit of a slip which the minister made in this connection. I understand he wrote to the

mayor of Winnipeg suggesting that his wife might come to the head of the lakes and christen the ship. It so happens that Mayor Coulter, although he is anxious to serve his country in every possible way, has been unable, I understand, to find a wife for the occasion. He happens to be a bachelor.
The hon. member said he was the only Winnipeg member in the. house. Is he aware that two Winnipeg members are on active service?
I thank my hon. friend for mentioning that fact. I had it in mind and intended to state it. while I was on my feet. I am grateful to him for mentioning it.

As one of the members who happen to have taken part, a rather inglorious part, -being merely blown out of a window in the Halifax explosion in 1917, having subsequently gone to sea on convoy duty, I wish to say one or two words on behalf of the men who are now carrying out this duty. In those days the convoy that left Halifax immediately after the explosion travelled at an official speed of four knots. Actually it was about three and one-half knots, or about a good walk. If anyone wants to know how long it would take to walk across the Atlantic, I may say that it would take thirty-one days, because that is how long we took on that convoy across the ocean. Eifty-seven ships went loaded with -munitions, ships similar to the Mont Blanc that blew up, one caught fire half way across the Atlantic, -and. we had to go and put out the fire. There is no job that requires the same constant vigilance, unseen and unsung, and the same attention to detail, as the convoy. There are few medals issued and many of the men do not get a chance for action. The success is measured by the delivery of the convoy to the other side. The other day Mr. Churchill said that a full ship delivered is a great deal more valuable than a ship -built. That can be easily understood when one visualizes what a ship can carry.
The minister has been twitted about matters of expenditure. There is an incident I always remember about my first trip to sea in an escort vessel with a convoy. We were battened down below decks; the watertight doors were shut, and I am free to admit that I was nervous. I was concerned about our chances if we were hit, and I asked the chief engineer, who was of course, Scotch, about this. He said to me, "My boy, the Germans are a sensible race; they know how much it costs to run this ship, and. they know she is far more use to them afloat than sunk, so that 72537-224
10, 1943
War Appropriation-Naval Services
there is no use in worrying". I suggest to the minister that he remember that when he is asked what it costs to run the navy.
There is a question I wish to ask with regard to our armed merchant cruisers. Is it the policy of the government to have a commodore with each convoy, and is that commodore a British or a Canadian officer? Do our armed merchant cruisers still go out with convoys? I know the Jervis Bay and other ships saw action at one time, but I should like to know if we -have armed merchant cruisers in our navy. My next question may have to do with the Minister of Munitions and Supply. For some time I have been seeing a number of mine-sweepers in a Toronto shipbuilding yard; I know them by number, if not by name, -because I have been passing them week after week. Why have these ships not reached tide-water? Is it on account of man-power? Why are they afloat but unfinished?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It would be only in the last month that a ship could leave Toronto for tide-water, because of ice conditions in the river and lake and canal.

They have been there
since last October.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Unless they were got out before the freeze-up they iwould have to stay all winter. It would not be on account of man-power, so far as we are concerned. There may be some question of machinery, and I shall find out about that. There is a commodore with every convoy, and so far as I know these are British officers. As to whether auxiliary cruisers and the like make up the escorts for convoys, I think that is. a matter I would have to discuss privately with my hon. friend.

I wish to thank the minister for having named two Canadian warships after two towns in my constituency. Great honour has been paid to the towns of Ganano-que and Brockville by making ships bearing those names an integral part of the Canadian -navy. It would do the minister's heart good to see the way in which the people of these towns have constituted themselves foster parents of these ships and the spirit with which they have organized to see that comforts are sent periodically to the men. I should like to enlarge upon the statement made by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) in whch he referred to two men from the corvette Oakville having boarded a German submarine. As I stated previously, one of



War Appropriation-Naval Services
these men came from Brockville, but I neglected to say that by now he probably wears the D.S.O.

There is the
greatest good-will toward the navy in Nova Scotia, as is evidenced by the comforts sent to the men of the navy by the ladies of the I.O.D.E. and other organizations. However, there is some criticism and misgiving about the time that some of'these ships spend in port undergoing repairs or for other causes. When the Cariboo which ran between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, and certain ore boats were sunk, many felt proper patrol had not been furnished. Yet navy vessels were tied up at the port of Halifax. I am not offering any criticism, but I think the minister should make a statement with regard to the cost of repairs and the time it takes to carry them out. The item we are now considering is for *167,571,202, and covers the upkeep of ships.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It
is impossible to keep a ship at sea for 365 days in the year, but there are people who think that should be done. Every time they see a ship at Halifax, Saint John or Sydney or in any other port they express surprise. It just cannot be done because ships must come in for a refit or repair, sometimes made necessary by enemy action, o:r sometimes by ordinary marine casualty. Instead of spending too much time in port, I think our men are being driven too much. Some have not been having the leave they should have. As my hon. friend knows, much of this repair work is carried on in private yards. A considerable strain has been placed upon these yards as well as upon our own dockyards. The skilled men are not available. When you enlarge an industry some twenty or thirty times, as we have the shipbuilding industry, you are bound to have a good deal of dilution; you will have many green men. The result is that repairs .are not carried on as rapidly as they would be in peace time when experienced shipwrights were available everywhere. I can say, however, that so far as we are concerned we are hastening the repairs of ships just as much as possible. We are not allowing ships to remain in ports any longer than is absolutely necessary, and so far as I know no sinkings have occurred anywhere through any carelessness or complacency in these respects.
Does the hon. member refer to ships being repaired at H.M.C. dockyards or the Halifax shipyard?

I made no special complaint about any particular yard.

I was referring to some misgivings that for some reason or another some of our ships have been in port when they should have been performing useful and necessary services in connection with convoy duties. Again I wish to point out that there is not the slightest reflection on the crews of these ships; there is the utmost good-will toward them on the part of people in the seaport towns of Nova Scotia, but I think it well to get an explanation and some reassurance from the minister that there is no cause for complaint in this regard.

I agree entirely with the thought expressed by the minister in regard to the time spent ashore by the crews of these ships. I was anxious to ascertain just what the hon. member for Cumberland had in mind in seeking this information, because I know that the workmen at both H.M.C. dockyard and the Halifax shipyard' are working at top speed practically all the time. It must be borne in mind also that many of the ships of the Canadian navy are old, particularly those which were turned over to us by the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Twenty-five years old.

They range from twenty-five tb thirty years old and require a great deal more attention than do the more modern ships. If I remember correctly, I believe it is estimated that they require something like thirty out of every ninety days for overhaul and general repair, which means that the average twenty-five-year old destroyer must spend one-third of the time in port being overhauled.
While I am on my feet I feel that as one member from the maritimes I should take exception to the attitude which has been exhibited by the hon. member for St. John-Al'bert. Like the minister, I was at a loss to follow the reasoning of the hon. member in his questions not only this evening but also a few days ago. He took exception to the amount of money being spent in the maritime provinces in construction, andi in general to the expenditures in connection with the expansion of the Royal Canadian Navy. It may be true that in New Brunswick not as much has been spent as the hon. member would like, but on the other hand an exceptionally large amount has been spent in Nova Scotia. Any member from the maritimes, or any member [DOT]who had an opportunity of visiting Nova Scotia in 1940 and viewing the work being done by the navy at H.M.C. dockyard, Halifax, would appreciate at once the common sense and reasonableness displayed by the officials of

War Appropriation-Naval Services
the navy department in making those expenditures there. It is the natural gateway for outgoing and incoming ships, both Canadian and British. Any hon. member would appreciate the manner in which convoys are assembled in Halifax harbour and Bedford basin, that great sheet of water four miles wide by six miles long where the combined fleets can assemble and manoeuvre at any time, where convoys can be drawn up and taken out to sea.
I say it does not become any member from the maritimes to be critical in regard to the expenditures in that part of Canada, which certainly is doing its part not only so far as the army is concerned but also, and principally, so far as the navy is concerned. I know that in the early days the navy department could not accept all those from the fishing villages who wished to join up; they were postponed time and again. With regard to enlistments in the army, the percentage figure for Nova Scotia is something like 44-1 per cent as against 12 per cent or as low as 9 per cent for some of the other provinces. So also have we made an exceptionally fine showing in regard to enlistments in the navy. Therefore I say to the minister that we appreciate the money that has been spent in Nova Scotia, and I do not believe the people of the maritimes will accept with good grace the statement of the hon. member for St. John-Albert, in somewhat slighting terms, that perhaps the fact that three ministers of the cabinet came from Nova Scotia accounted for the large amount of money spent in that province. I say it is a credit to Nova Scotia to have in the cabinet three men such as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald). I think it is to the credit of any province that it can produce such men. Instead of criticizing the efforts of one particular minister from the maritimes, I think every maritime member should be ready to compliment the minister upon the excellent work he is doing for Canada.
If the hour were not so late, Mr. Chairman, I should like to offer one or two further observations. I do not know whether or not this item will be carried over until to-morrow, but perhaps I might proceed to present one or two criticisms or rather suggestions. Coming up on the train a short time ago, I talked with a number of ratings, who questioned the wisdom of the minister's statement with respect to the use of aircraft carriers in a navy such as ours. I do not wish to hold up the estimates, so that I shall proceed 72537-2241
to enlarge upon this thought as quickly as possible; it is offered to the minister not as expert opinion but rather so that he might think it over. It is suggested that instead of an expenditure such as would be entailed in connection with an aircraft carrier, the money would be better invested in a cruiser or cruisers or in high-powered tribal-class destroyers, such as we are now adding to the navy. A craft more powerful and faster can carry out the duties which I believe rests with this country,, namely, that of convoying and defending the ships which are carrying munitions and supplies and troops overseas. I could enlarge on that to a great extent, but the hour is late, and I shall reserve anything further until a later date. I thought, however, I should at least take my stand in support of the minister, who is doing his best. The people of Nova Scotia know he is doing his best to bring about the object for which we are all striving, namely that Canada may have a navy of which she may be justly proud.
l^Ir. HAZEN:	The senior member for
Halifax (Mr. Isnor) has just made reference to my remarks in the house on Tuesday afternoon or evening in connection with the discrimination shown against New Brunswick by this government, since the commencement of the war. He takes exception to my attitude.
General attitude.
My general attitude. He is at a loss to understand just why I should protest and why I should demand, on behalf of my province, that it get a fair share of war activities and war expenditures.
You would be slow if you did not protest.

As a member representing a New Brunswick constituency I have the absolute right to protest. And I will add that so long as this discrimination continues I propose to rise in my place in the house on every available opportunity and protest against this obvious discrimination. In making my protest I do not have to cite any prejudiced or partisan authorities. The other evening I quoted a statement by the Hon. J. B. McNair, premier of New Brunswick and a supporter of this government. This is what he said on June 5 of last year:
I am sure that the people of New Brunswick . will persist in doing their bit. But the sooner however the tactics of discrimination and' favouritism are abandoned, the better.
I concur absolutely in his remarks. The sooner the tactics of discrimination and favouritism are abandoned, the better. Thirty million dollars spent by the navy department

War Appropriation-Naval Services
since the outbreak of war for the erection of buildings and the purchase of land in Nova Scotia; yes, thirty millions of dollars, in the province from which the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services and the Minister of Finance cornel Of course there is no politics in that! Oh, no, we are all above anything like that! Nobody would think of anything like that in this house-Liberals on that side of the house, or Liberals in Nova Scotia! Nobody would think of anything like that! But just the same, thirty millions of dollars were spent in Nova Scotia, while during the same time in New Brunswick it spent just $19,000!
Am I justified in protesting about discrimination and unfairness of that kind? While New Brunswick is not quite as large as Nova Scotia, yet it is nearly as large, and in every way it has contributed its fair share to the furtherance of the war effort. Have I no right to protest when discrimination of that kind exists? I repeat what I said last night, that if Ripley, the cartoonist, whose drawings appear every day in the newspapers, were furnished with these figures, he would have material for another illuminating cartoon.
I do not wish to repeat everything I said the other night. The senior member from Halifax may be at a loss to understand my attitude. But let me tell him this-and he may take it to heart-that the people of New Brunswick will not be at a loss to understand my attitude, and the stand I have taken in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: And thereby hangs a tale.

Thereby hangs a tale, yes; and it will be more than a "tail" that will hang, I can tell you, at the next election.
Let me say to the senior member for Halifax that I do not envy Nova Scotia anything she gets, or anything to which she is justly and fairly entitled. At an earlier session I ' spoke on the floor of the house about the lack of assistance and the lack of contracts for war munitions and supplies awarded not only to New Brunswick, but to Nova Scotia as well. Time does not permit my looking up my remarks, or making reference to what I said on that occasion. But at that time I spoke not only for New Brunswick but for Nova Scotia. I was speaking for the maritime provinces. On that occasion I quoted from the Rowell-Sirois report the statement that New Brunswick shares with Nova Scotia the unhappy distinction of having the most unfavourable economic history of any part of Canada since confederation. The statement made by the commission at that time was, I believe, correct.
C&tr. Hazen.]
It is only as the maritime provinces stand together and work in their own interests that conditions will ever be improved.
But, sir, that is one thing. It is another thing for me to rise in my place in the house and protest against the lack of capital assistance received by New Brunswick for war industries; the lack of assistance we have been given in other respects; the manner in which we have been disregarded in connection with the establishment of air fields, air establishments, military establishments and naval establishments since the war commenced.
I do not wish to read into the record what I said the other night. For the present I shall let the matter remain as it is.
There are one or two questions that I asked the minister which he has not yet answered.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
